entries.title: Judge halts South Side plant operations over city, state's foul odor lawsuit
entries.summary: <p>A judge ordered the temporary halt of operations at a South Side animal feed plant that has been the source of hundreds of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2025/07/09/pullman-innovations-odor-pollution-violations-chicago-health-epa-peter-chico" target="_blank" ><u>complaints over putrid odors</u></a> for years.</p><p>Judge Thomas Donnelly granted a temporary restraining order in favor of the Illinois Attorney General’s office and the city of Chicago, which <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/08/05/attorney-general-city-lawsuit-against-pullman-innovations-odors-kwame-raoul" target="_blank" ><u>sued </u></a>Pullman Innovations in August over the odors, alleging violations of state and city air pollution laws. </p><p>The business makes an additive in animal feed used by farmers who supply eggs to food company Dutch Farms.</p><p>In a statement Wednesday, Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul said the plant shouldn’t reopen until it “addresses the odors and air pollution and comes into compliance with Illinois’ environmental laws.”</p><p>The legal order bars the plant from operating until at least January 14, when a hearing is scheduled for Raoul and the city’s motion for a preliminary injunction. Operations would be halted until a final order is issued.</p><p>“Members of the community around the Pullman Innovations facility have carried too heavy a burden of environmental harm for too long, and I am pleased that they will finally have some relief from the foul odors that were interrupting their lives and harming their ability to enjoy their homes and neighborhood activities,” Raoul said.</p><p>A lawyer for Pullman Innovations parent company, A-F Acquisition, LLC didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>The plant has spurred complaints since before Pullman Innovations took over, including some that stretch back decades to a predecessor company, Agri-Fine, which was previously sued by former Attorney General Lisa Madigan before it went out of business.</p><p>The Chicago Department of Public Health has previously ticketed Pullman Innovations multiple times for code violations. Illinois EPA investigators have also previously confirmed the smell both inside the plant and in the surrounding neighborhoods, at times making it hard for them to breathe.</p><p>One city inspector, whose testimony was offered in support of the restraining order, said he personally had conducted 160 inspections at the site and described the smell as a “foul rotten egg, sulfur odor” that “caused my nostrils to burn and gave me an acute headache.”</p><p>Some neighbors <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/08/14/south-chicago-chapel-funeral-home-smell-pollution-pullman-innovations-odor-southeast-side-south-deering-steel-mills" target="_blank" ><u>suggested to the Chicago Sun-Times</u></a> in August that the overwhelming odor might have masked the smell of decomposing bodies at the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/grave-injustice/2026/10/14/55-decomposing-bodies-found-in-south-chicago-chapel-identified" target="_blank" ><u>South Chicago Chapel funeral home</u></a>, which is currently under investigation.</p>

entries.title: Evanston/Skokie School District 65 proposes closure of 2 elementary schools
entries.summary: <p>Evanston/Skokie School District 65 administrators revealed a plan to close Lincolnwood and Dewey Elementary Schools amid a budget-balancing proposal that would also impact attendance boundaries, shutter child care and early childhood development programs.</p><p>District officials revealed the details of the previously announced plan at a board meeting Tuesday night to suggest retaining school properties as a "long-term facility strategy and vision for the future," which could include using them as flex schools or repairing them in the future.</p><p>Evanston/Skokie School District 65 Assistant Superintendent Stacy Beardsley said Lincolnwood was chosen because Haven Middle School feeder schools require the most capital investment while seeing a 33% decline in enrollment. </p><p>Most of its students would be absorbed into Willard Elementary School while Dewey Elementary School students would largely be transferred to Lincoln Elementary School, administrators said. </p><p>The proposed closures and boundary changes would save around $2.9 million annually, but force more than 700 students to switch schools, including some who had just moved to Lincolnwood after Kingsley Elementary School closed last year.</p><p>"We have confidence that this footprint is the right size for the district for the next decade," Beardsley said. "The long-term plan for the Lincolnwood School would be to secure a referendum to build a modernized Lincolnwood School that could better meet the needs of our students today."</p><p>The proposal also seeks to end the School Age Child Care program at the end of this school year, which administrators said cost $1.95 million and would need a 35% increase in what the district charged parents to break even. It also called for phasing out the district's Head Start and Early Start programs by 2029, which officials said cost more than $2 million annually. </p><p>The closures and program reductions also mean the elimination of nearly 90 certified teachers and 129 support roles cut, along with eight administrators.</p><p>In finding additional revenue streams, District 65 Chief Financial Officer Eric Miller proposed raising the student registration fee by $100 for students who don't qualify for free or reduced lunches due to financial hardship.</p><p>A vote is scheduled for Nov. 9. Administrators also will also push for a ballot initiative added to the docket for 2028 which would allow residents to vote on the allocation of funds for the properties and renovations for existing schools.</p><p>Interim Superintendent Eric Witherspoon said if the board approved the plan, it would "be the last time that you see a proposal [to close schools] in this community."</p><p>"There have been so many discussions and proposals and efforts to try to deal with our deficit, but we haven't solved it, and we haven't solved it because we have not gone directly at the structural issues," Witherspoon said.</p><p>Last month, officials announced the plans to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/09/18/evanston-skokie-parents-fear-impact-hope-for-stability-as-district-looks-to-cut-20-million-close-2-schools" >close at least two of 16 schools</a> and shave $20 million from the budget, though they had yet to announce which schools would be targeted.</p><p>It's the latest in a series of school closures over the last several years. </p><p>Last year, <a class="Link" href="https://evanstonroundtable.com/2026/06/05/kingsley-elementary-school-closed/" target="_blank" >Kingsley Elementary School</a> was shuttered amid a prolonged debate — which, at the time, prevented Lincolnwood Elementary from closing — ultimately cutting $6 million in operational costs. In 2024, the board voted to close the Dr. Bessie Rhodes School of Global Studies, <a class="Link" href="https://evanstonroundtable.com/2026/06/05/bessie-rhodes-closed-last-day/" target="_blank" >which shut its doors last June</a>.</p><p>At the Tuesday meeting, Beardsley said the school closures of two schools last year saved the district $3 million. She also claimed the move saved the district $57 million in repairs over the next 20 years, though in its cost breakdowns, staffing remained the largest portion of savings.</p><p>When pressed by board members, Beardsley said increased transportation cost projections weren't yet available, and that she would have to come back to the board with answers on how special education would be impacted.</p><p>“The path that drove us to budget deficits and student enrollment decline was paved by us,” said board member Maria Opdycke. “This is a situation of our own making.”</p><p>Board President Nichole Pinkard also briefly addressed the recent guilty plea from former District 65 superintendent Devon Horton on federal wire fraud, embezzlement and tax charges related </p><p>Earlier in the day, two former Chicago Public Schools employees <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/10/13/former-cps-employees-plea-guilty-to-federal-fraud-charges-in-district-contract-kickback-scheme" >also plead guilty</a> to creating companies to apply as vendors for professional service contracts with Evanston/Skokie District 65 by submitting “false and fraudulent” documents to win more than $100,000. They then hid thousands of dollars in kickbacks to Horton, according to federal prosecutors.</p><p></p><p>"The convergence of this report and Dr. Horton’s guilty plea reminds the board that rebuilding trust requires more than statements," Pinkard said. "It requires accountability in how we oversee this district, make decisions, and communicate with the people we serve. And it requires vigilance in our execution of these duties."</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/10/13/former-cps-employees-plea-guilty-to-federal-fraud-charges-in-district-contract-kickback-scheme" >Former Hyde Park Academy principal, AD plead guilty in contract fraud scheme</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/09/18/evanston-skokie-parents-fear-impact-hope-for-stability-as-district-looks-to-cut-20-million-close-2-schools" >Evanston-Skokie parents fear impact as district looks to cut $20 million, close 2 schools</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: 4 takeaways from CPS School Board president forum
entries.summary: <p>With just three weeks until Election Day, the three candidates vying to become the first elected Chicago School Board president sharpened the choices for voters by offering up distinct views on a range of topics, from school ratings to potential school closings to dealing with the school district’s struggling finances, at a forum sponsored by WBEZ, the Chicago Sun-Times and Chalkbeat Chicago on Wednesday.</p><p>And in a surprise show of unity, two of the candidates, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/hilario-dominguez/" target="_blank" ><u>Hilario Dominguez</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/victor-p-henderson/" target="_blank" ><u>Victor Henderson</u></a>, accused their opponent <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/jessica-biggs/" target="_blank" ><u>Jessica Biggs</u></a> of resurfacing controversies to harm both their campaigns.</p><p>Here are four take-aways from the forum, which included questions from an audience of students from Gwendolyn Brooks College Prep High School, a Chicago public school in Roseland.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/MQI08GaQpmI?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Chicago School Board president candidates meet for forum ahead of 2026 election"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p><h3>Blame game on campaign controversies</h3><p>Each candidate has baggage their opponents have called disqualifying, but on Wednesday Henderson and Dominguez blamed Biggs for controversies that have followed their campaigns.</p><p>Dominguez, former deputy political director for the Chicago Teachers Union, has been in the spotlight after the CPS Inspector General <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/10/09/reopened-probe-into-cps-board-president-candidates-alleged-inappropriate-contact-with-teen-could-end-soon" target="_blank" ><u>reopened an investigation</u></a> into whether he behaved inappropriately with a 17-year-old in 2017 while working as a community organizer before becoming a teacher. Dominguez denies the allegations and calls them politically motivated.</p><p>After the forum taping, WBEZ confirmed that CPS’ inspector general closed the investigation. In a letter to Dominguez, the IG’s office said it determined that there is <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/10/14/cps-watchdog-closes-investigation-of-school-board-candidate-with-no-actionable-finding-of-sexual-misconduct" target="_blank" ><u>“no actionable finding of sexual misconduct</u></a>.”</p><p>Meanwhile Henderson, a defense attorney, has faced questions <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/09/22/school-board-president-candidate-victor-henderson-defends-disciplining-his-children-says-school-staff-should-never-use-corporal-punishment" target="_blank" ><u>about corporal punishment</u></a> after divorce papers came to light in which his ex-wife accused him of hitting his son. Henderson denies ever abusing his children.</p><p>Henderson accused Biggs’ campaign of surfacing the controversies.</p><p>“Information has come to me that Jessica Biggs is the person who's trying to drag both me and Hilario through the mud,” Henderson said.</p><p>Biggs, a former CPS principal, denied the charge and said her opponents were trying to deflect difficult questions.</p><p>“I guess I shouldn't be surprised that men who have allegations around sexual harassment, around spousal abuse, domestic violence would choose to blame me for their infractions,” Biggs said. “It’s really disappointing that people can't just take accountability for their actions.”</p><p>Biggs, who was <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/09/23/chicago-school-board-member-jessica-biggs-faces-scrutiny-over-2018-firing-as-she-runs-for-presidents-seat" target="_blank" ><u>fired from her position as a CPS</u></a> principal, has faced her own questions about being taken off the district’s Do Not Hire list. That came after she won a school board seat two years ago.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Different approaches on school closures</h3><p>A moratorium on school closures expires at the end of this school year, and candidates <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/09/17/should-chicago-close-more-schools-candidates-for-school-board-president-diverge-on-key-issue" target="_blank" ><u>diverge on how the district should handle schools with few students</u></a>. Enrollment this year has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/09/24/chicago-public-schools-enrollment-drops-by-more-than-11-000-accelerating-long-term-downward-trend" target="_blank" ><u>dropped by 11,500 students </u></a>to its lowest number in more than two decades.</p><p>Dominguez, a former special education teacher, is the only candidate who has committed not to close any schools and wants to extend the moratorium. He contends that closures disproportionately harm Black and Brown students, and pointed to research showing that <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/06/15/shootings-increased-near-chicagos-closed-schools-that-sat-empty-study-finds" target="_blank" ><u>violence increased in areas around shuttered schools</u></a>.</p><p>He favors repurposing space in underutilized schools for mental clinics, food pantries and other services. “I understand that there may be red tape and difficulties and obstacles in figuring out how to build these partnerships,” Dominguez said. “But those are the things that we work on as a school board president.”</p><p>Henderson on our <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/victor-p-henderson/" target="_blank" ><u>candidate questionnaire</u></a> said he supports school closings as an “extraordinary last resort.” And on Wednesday, he said it doesn’t “necessarily make sense” to keep “all” the buildings open. He said the district can’t be afraid to discuss the matter when the moratorium expires. “That’s why CPS is in such dire shape, because they’ve avoided hard conversations,” he said. “You have to sit with the community, you have to figure it out.”</p><p>Biggs, who was a principal when there were mass closures in 2013 and said the impact was “exceptionally harmful” and long-lasting. She did not rule out closing schools but said the community needs to be involved in the decision-making process.</p><p>She said previous closures were made top-down and if the district considers shutting down or consolidating schools it needs to first develop a plan alongside the community on what to do with empty buildings.</p><p>“Anything that we’re building has to come from an express interest from people who are going to be using those spaces,” said Biggs, who now runs a program that brings healthcare and social services to Chicago public schools.</p><div class="Enhancement" </div><p></p><h3>What’s the plan to fill CPS’ budget gaps? </h3><p>On the campaign trail and in their platforms, Biggs and Henderson respectively stress financial stability and financial responsibility while Dominguez is tightly focused on boosting CPS’ budget by bringing home more revenue from the state.</p><p>On Wednesday, all three were asked how they handle a potentially looming budget crisis.</p><p>The current board <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/07/31/what-does-the-new-uncertain-budget-mean-for-schools/" target="_blank" ><u>approved a budget in July</u></a> that counts on hundreds of millions from the state and city that isn’t guaranteed. If it <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/08/24/cps-first-day-of-school/" target="_blank" ><u>doesn’t come through this fall</u></a>, that could mean a midyear budget freeze or potentially layoffs. That would be at the top of the new president’s agenda when they are installed in January.</p><p>Biggs <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/07/31/seeking-to-reverse-layoffs-chicago-school-board-approves-budget-assuming-more-state-money-will-come/" target="_blank" ><u>voted against the measure</u></a> that assumed CPS would get more state money, a decision she said she was “really proud of” during Wednesday’s forum. She cited her past experience as a CPS principal who faced layoffs and furloughs from the district as the reason why she wanted to take “a clear stance against assuming revenue that is not available to us.”</p><p>Henderson largely aligned with Biggs’ stance, saying CPS can’t “create a budget based on money that hasn’t arrived.” He also railed against <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/chicago-school-board/2026/10/13/long-a-foregone-conclusion-property-tax-hikes-will-no-longer-be-a-given-under-elected-cps-board" target="_blank" ><u>raising property taxes each year</u></a> to maximum, which CPS consistently does and Biggs has approved as a current board member. Dominguez said he supports the annual increase and Biggs says she does not. Henderson says voters shouldn’t “pay another dime” without auditing CPS’ expenditures.</p><p>Dominguez differentiated himself from his opponents the most by praising the board’s choice to halt staff layoffs. He also mentioned his ongoing conversations with Springfield lawmakers to pledge additional money to CPS. I don't want any powerful unions like the CTU or SEIU pulling my strings.”</p><p>Dominguez didn’t shy away from CTU’s support, saying “folks should be proud of having the support of those educators.” His pride in CTU’s endorsement didn’t come without a jab, alleging that Henderson had “wore that suit” when he asked for the union’s support earlier on this election cycle.</p><p>Taking a less combative approach, Biggs said the various donors to her campaign, which include SEIU, which represent CPS support staff, just prove her ability to organize a “diverse coalition.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-880000" name="module-880000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>More CPS School Board coverage</b><br><br>WBEZ and the Chicago Sun-Times have created resources to help voters prepare for this fall’s historic Chicago School Board election. entries.title: Bulls' Noa Essengue looking to prove he can be a physical player
entries.summary: <p>MILWAUKEE — The message couldn’t have been delivered any clearer.</p><p>There was no yelling or screaming even needed from <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls" >Bulls</a> coach Tiago Splitter.</p><p>Just a simple announcement of the second half starting lineup in the July Summer League game. A lineup that no longer included Noa Essengue.</p><p>Splitter, who wanted to coach the first two Summer League games to set a tone, explained his decision for the benching afterward, pointing out that the second-year forward just wasn’t playing with any physicality. A no-no in his book.</p><p>Message received.</p><p>“I think it was a strong message,” Essengue said on Wednesday, looking back to the summer. “I didn’t play at all last year (because of shoulder surgery) so I was hoping I would play a lot this year. And to see my playing time cut in Summer League because they said I don’t put any force or energy on the court, it was something where it just forces you to change it, to put that force out there. Do what you need to force them to put you on the court.”</p><p>That’s what he’s been trying to focus on throughout training camp and the preseason games.</p><p>His coach has taken notice.</p><p>“Honestly, Noa, he’s playing hard. He’s trying to do everything we ask,” Splitter said. “I think there were two situations where we were kind of like, ‘Noa, we’ve got to be better here.’ Other than that, he’s trying to do the right things, crashing the offensive boards, being aggressive on defense, that’s what you ask from a young guy.”</p><p>Not an easy ask, especially if it’s not in Essengue’s nature to play a physical brand of basketball. Coming from the German League, the No. 12 overall pick from the 2025 draft was only 18 when he was selected and wasn’t exactly known for his physicality growing up in France.</p><p>While it feels like a trait of you either have it or you don’t, Essengue doesn’t see it that way.</p><p>“I think it’s something you can learn easily,” Essengue said. “When you go to a new league where most all of the players are older than you, they’re going to naturally play more physical. You have to try and adapt to that, adapt yourself so you can be ready.”</p><p>Something he is still yet to prove on a consistent basis. That’s why he’s in a competition for a rotation spot with the likes of Patrick Williams and Leonard Miller.</p><p>“I’m a competitor. I love to compete for everything, on the court, off the court, I love competing,” Essengue added. “Yeah, I was a first-round pick, PWill was No. 4 (overall in 2020), Lenny is in the last year of his contract, so we’re all playing for something.”</p><p></p><h3><b>Nic of time</b></h3><p></p><p>Splitter was still holding out hope that Zach Collins (quad) and Tobe Awaka (knee) would both be ready for the start of the regular season next week, but time is running out on Nic Claxton and his injured hamstring, especially since he’s missed most of camp.</p><p>“You just got to be careful with those hamstrings,” Splitter said. “We know that there is a high chance of doing it again, so we’ve got to be real careful in bringing him back.</p><p>“What I know is right before the season we’re going to evaluate him again, see where he’s at, and then give you guys a timeline.”</p><p></p><h3><b>Final dress rehearsal</b></h3><h3></h3><p></p><p>The Bulls will close out the preseason on Friday when they host Minnesota, and Splitter planned to continue playing most of the starters — if healthy — to continue getting the roster up to speed with the high tempo style he wants to play.</p><p>“We need to get some guys to go up and down, get some game rhythm,” he said.</p>

entries.title: 18-year-old woman dies after being shot in head in Belmont Cragin
entries.summary: <p>An 18-year-old woman died after being shot in the head Wednesday night in the Belmont Cragin neighborhood, Chicago police said. </p><p>Police at about 8:53 p.m. responded to a residence in the 2700 block of South Monitor Avenue and found the woman with a gunshot wound to the head. </p><p>She was taken by ambulance to Loyola University Medical Center, where she later died, police said. </p><p>Area 5 detectives are investigating. </p>

entries.title: Fire can't slow down streaking Union
entries.summary: <p>Bruno Damiani netted two goals after Milan Iloski scored — all with a man advantage — and Cavan Sullivan set a record for teenagers as the Philadelphia Union beat the Chicago Fire 3-1 on Wednesday night at Soldier Field for their eighth straight victory in a club-record 14-match unbeaten streak.</p><p>Sullivan, who turned 17 this season, picked up his 14th assist on Damiani's first goal to set a league record for teens with 21 goal contributions this season.</p><p>Philadelphia (13-10-6) has gone 12-0-2 under interim coach Ryan Richter after he replaced Bradley Carnell at the end of May during the World Cup break. The Union started the day in sixth place after sitting last in the Eastern Conference before the coaching change.</p><p>Maren Haile-Selassie staked Chicago (14-9-6) to a 1-0 halftime lead with a goal in the 44th minute, but defender Jack Elliott was tagged with a yellow card in the 41st minute and again in the first minute of stoppage time, leaving the Fire a man down from there with his red-card exit.</p><p>Noah Allen and Jonathan Bamba had assists on Haile-Selassie's 11th goal of the campaign.</p><p>Iloski found the net four minutes into the second half to tie it 1-1. It was his sixth goal in the last four matches and his 18th of the season.</p><p>Damiani added the go-ahead score in the 55th minute and an insurance goal in the 67th, giving the striker 11 netters this season.</p><p>Damiani and defender Frankie Westfield had assists on Iloski's equalizer. Iloski joined Sullivan with an assist on Damiani's first netter and Jovan Lukic snagged one on his second goal.</p><p>Andre Blake stopped three shots on goal for Philadelphia.</p><p>Chris Brady finished with four saves for Chicago, which saw a three-match win streak end.</p><p>The Fire beat the Union 2-1 on the road to close out March.</p><p>Chicago falls to 9-5-1 at home, while Philadelphia improves to 5-7-2 on the road.</p><p>The Union haven't lost since a 6-4 setback on the road at Inter Miami on May 24.</p><p><b>Up next</b></p><p>Philadelphia: Hosts Charlotte FC on Saturday.</p><p>Chicago: At New England Revolution on Saturday.</p>
entries.author: AP

entries.title: Bulls would love to see versatile big Jalen Smith continue spacing out
entries.summary: <p>MILWAUKEE — Jalen Smith is headed for a nice payday.</p><p>Whether it’s with the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls" target="_blank" >Bulls</a> or another team this upcoming offseason is yet to be determined, but the seven-year veteran is being set up to grab a bag next summer.</p><p>At least Bulls coach Tiago Splitter hopes that’s the case because that would mean his plan for how to use Smith during the 2026-27 season was executed to perfection.</p><p>Splitter detailed the Smith factor in the Bulls’ 125-104 victory Wednesday against the Bucks, discussing the shortage of centers the team has been dealing with this preseason and how Smith could be the answer to address that deficiency even when Nic Claxton (hamstring) and Zach Collins (quad) return.</p><p>“What I see from [Smith] is he’s a guy that can stretch the floor,” Splitter said. “Having a five that can stretch the floor and create space is tremendous, so you’ve got to try to use that as an advantage, and we go from there.”</p><p>Case in point: The first half against the Bucks. The Bulls outscored Milwaukee 62-39, and Smith was a big reason why. Playing center — despite being built like a stretch four — Smith led the Bulls with 11 points on 3-for-3 shooting from three-point range, grabbed five rebounds and blocked a shot. He finished with 15 points in just over 20 minutes.</p><p>But the numbers aren’t even the biggest benefit Smith provides.</p><p>Because he shot 37.3% from three-point range last season and 42.4% from long range in 2023-24, the scouting report says he’s a deep threat. That’s what Splitter wants. With athletic forwards Matas Buzelis, Caleb Wilson and Lenny Miller, Splitter wants opposing centers pulled out to challenge Smith. That’s just clearing the runway for the air show.</p><p>There aren’t many opposing teams with forwards as springy as the Bulls have, so Buzelis and Wilson have a chance to play downhill and attack the rim.</p><p>“They look at me as a spacer,” Smith said after the game. “So being able to hit open shots, create more space, create more lobs for Josh [Giddey], Norm [Powell], Matas, Caleb, they like getting downhill. And, obviously, being an offensive-rebound threat, that creates more kick-outs for them. Teams are so spaced out for me with their fives, no one is protecting the paint. It’s the best of both worlds for me here.”</p><p>Against Milwaukee, Smith also was involved in a lot of high pick-and-roll/pick-and-pop plays with Giddey, especially to start the second half.</p><p>Even with a healthy Claxton and Collins, three centers are almost a must because of how much Splitter wants to run.</p><p>Continuing to push Wilson’s development is also a must, but one that Splitter admitted doesn’t need much pushing. Wilson had 10 points after a slow start.</p><p>The prized rookie continues to be one of the hardest workers on the roster, often the first one in the facility in the morning and the last one out at night.</p><p>And while he has been playing with more consistency since the preseason opener, the scary news for the opposition is the NBA game already is slowing down for him.</p><p>For a rookie to be talking like that after less than a handful of preseason games says a lot. Splitter believes his work ethic and film study also speak volumes.</p><p>“There’s a lot of teaching, especially with young guys,” Splitter said. “Caleb is a smart kid; he’s picking it up quick. Yeah, he’s learning, and he’s eager to understand what we’re doing and to learn.”</p>

entries.title: Woman, 95, killed in 3 vehicle chain-reaction wreck in Pilsen
entries.summary: <p>A three vehicle chain-reaction crash left a 95-year-old woman dead Wednesday evening on the Lower West Side. </p><p>Guadalupe Almendarez, 95, was westbound in a grey car when it rear-ended a black truck stopped at a light about 5:35 p.m. in the 1900 block of West 18th Street. The collision caused the truck to hit a silver car also stopped at the light, police said. </p><p>Almendarez, of the Clearing neighborhood, was taken to Stroger Hospital initially in critical condition, but she was pronounced dead at 7:54 p.m., according to the Cook County medical examiner's office. </p><p>No one else hurt and the Major Accidents Investigation Unit is probing the crash. </p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Father appalled as daughter leads on admiring classmate
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My wife and I are the proud parents of a popular, beautiful, charming and usually well-meaning 16-year-old girl. However, some of her recent behavior is causing serious concern.</p><p>"Lindsey" is part of her class's "in" crowd. Still, she's engaging and friendly to everyone, which is a value my wife and I have worked to instill in her. One boy, "Henry," is sweet on her. In short, Henry is not exactly in her social circle. He's quiet, but he gets excellent grades and is considerate and respectful.</p><p>Lindsey has been giving Henry the impression that she is romantically interested even though she isn't. As a result, he's helped her with many school projects, among other favors. She often has him over to maintain the charade. I've gotten to know Henry, and I genuinely like him. He's a good kid, and I'm disgusted at Lindsey's behavior.</p><p>I tried to talk to Lindsey about it, and she said she's "just using what God gave her" to better her life. She seems to think that if Henry is happy being around her, she's not doing anything wrong. I feel I should talk to Henry about this, or at least his parents. What do you think? I love my daughter, but I don't want her taking advantage of (and possibly destroying) this young man's heart! — <i>DOUBTING DAD</i></p><p><b>DEAR DAD:</b> Henry may be happy now, but you and Lindsey both know he'll be crushed when the truth comes out. This must end immediately. Inform Lindsey that if she doesn't come clean and sincerely apologize to Henry, there will be consequences. Be prepared to follow through in whatever way you would normally discipline a self-centered, misbehaving child.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I've had a college friend for more than 45 years. We've had some issues over the years. Because I have a bit of a temper, she has said numerous times that I belong in a mental institution. We had another disagreement several months ago and have ceased all communication. She spoke to me in the tone of voice you would use to talk to a 2-year-old.</p><p>I'm now having some medical issues she and her husband are not aware of. We are not young anymore. My dilemma is this: If she or her husband passes, do I go to the funeral? I now use a walker, and if their church's chair lift is broken, I would be unable to attend the service anyway. I live quite a distance away. — <i>ESTRANGED FRIEND IN NEW HAMPSHIRE</i></p><p><b>DEAR FRIEND:</b> Nowhere did you indicate that this friend is having health issues. In light of your long friendship, she should be made aware that you are unwell. Tell her you would not want your long friendship to end as things stand.</p><p>Funerals are intended as a support for the living. If you would like to attend when the inevitable does occur, contact the person who will conduct the service and ask if the funeral home or house of worship is ADA accessible. There's no need to stay home due to what might go wrong.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: Judicial tide may be turning against indiscriminate Flock mass surveillance
entries.summary: <p>Back in 1983, the Supreme Court <a class="Link" href="https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/460/276/" target="_blank" >declared</a> that "a person traveling in an automobile on public thoroughfares has no reasonable expectation of privacy in his movements from one place to another." That increasingly doubtful proposition underpins a nationwide network of <a class="Link" href="https://deflock.org/" target="_blank" >more than 144,000</a> artificial intelligence-assisted cameras that <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/08/31/the-belated-backlash-against-flock-cameras/" target="_blank" >tracks</a> the travels of innocent motorists across the country billions of times each week.</p><p>So far, state and federal courts have almost uniformly rejected constitutional challenges to automated license plate readers installed by companies such as <a class="Link" href="https://www.flocksafety.com/" target="_blank" >Flock Safety</a>. But in a <a class="Link" href="https://cbs12.com/resources/pdf/c40b1aac-12c1-4633-9953-a64475102296-USVKYLE.pdf" target="_blank" >decision</a> that could signal a shift in the legal treatment of Flock cameras, a federal judge in Oklahoma recently <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/10/07/judge-says-warrantless-flock-search-violated-drivers-fourth-amendment-rights/" target="_blank" >recognized</a> that they enable "a type of indiscriminate mass surveillance."</p><p>License plate readers are much more sophisticated than the technology that the Supreme Court considered in 1983, when it approved the warrantless use of a radio transmitter that helped police tail a suspected methamphetamine manufacturer's car. Three decades later, by contrast, the court <a class="Link" href="https://tile.loc.gov/storage-services/service/ll/usrep/usrep565/usrep565400/usrep565400.pdf" target="_blank" >said</a> police should have obtained a search warrant before attaching a GPS tracker to another drug suspect's car.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-120000" name="module-120000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>The majority opinion in the latter case emphasized the physical intrusion necessary to install the tracker. But five justices embraced an alternative rationale, saying GPS tracking impinges on <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/07/08/the-supreme-courts-reasonable-expectation-of-privacy-test-defies-expectations/" target="_blank" >reasonable expectations of privacy</a> by revealing potentially sensitive information about the target's historical whereabouts.</p><p>That theory came to the fore in a 2018 <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2018/06/22/scotus-rejects-warrantless-tracking-of-c/" target="_blank" >case</a> involving mobile-phone location data collected by cell sites, which the majority <a class="Link" href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/17pdf/16-402_h315.pdf" target="_blank" >said</a> implicated the Fourth Amendment because "individuals have a reasonable expectation of privacy in the whole of their physical movements." The Supreme Court <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/06/29/in-big-win-for-fourth-amendment-advocates-the-supreme-court-says-geofence-warrants-count-as-a-search/" target="_blank" >reiterated</a> that principle this year, extending it to data collected by Google's location history feature.</p><p>"An individual has a reasonable expectation of privacy in records about his cell phone's location," Justice Elena Kagan <a class="Link" href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/25-112_0am4.pdf" target="_blank" >said</a> in the majority opinion, "and police intrude on that constitutionally protected interest when they demand the information." By similar logic, U.S. District Judge Sara E. Hill <a class="Link" href="https://cbs12.com/resources/pdf/c40b1aac-12c1-4633-9953-a64475102296-USVKYLE.pdf" target="_blank" >concluded</a> this month in the Oklahoma case, people have a reasonable expectation of privacy in license plate reader records, and police therefore generally need a warrant to search them.</p><p>Those databases include "information about all vehicles that pass by any network-connected camera at all times," which police can peruse "on demand," Hill noted. "Freedom from persistent, dragnet-style surveillance while in public is not a foreign concept in our society, and it is a reasonable expectation that society already accepts," as reflected in the Supreme Court's cellphone decisions.</p><p>Like cars, cellphones "move in public places where people can see you in plain view," Hill wrote. "But it becomes constitutionally problematic when law enforcement can indiscriminately and passively catalog your whereabouts over an extended period of time and then use that information for any purpose whenever convenient."</p><p>At this point, Hill's decision is an outlier.</p><p>"It appears that nearly every court examining the issue to date has determined that license plate reader technology use is not a search under the Fourth Amendment because people have no reasonable expectation of privacy in their movements on public streets," she noted.</p><p>Last month, for instance, a federal judge in California <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/volokh/2026/09/16/use-of-flock-cameras-is-not-a-fourth-amendment-search-district-court-rules/" target="_blank" >held</a> that license plate reader database searches are "clearly distinguishable from and less extensive than the 'near perfect surveillance' achievable" with cell-site or location history data.</p><p>And the day after Hill's ruling, a state judge in California <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/SIREN-v.-Joseph-10-2-26.pdf" target="_blank" >rejected</a> a challenge to San Jose's Flock camera network, saying "there is no reasonable expectation of privacy in license plate data collected from cameras directed solely at public streets."</p><p>A <a class="Link" href="https://ij.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Doc.-1-Complaint-for-Declaratory-and-Injunctive-Relief.pdf" target="_blank" >federal lawsuit</a> involving the same city's license plate reader system, which the Institute for Justice <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/04/16/san-joses-creepy-and-deeply-intrusive-alpr-camera-system-is-unconstitutional-a-new-lawsuit-says/" target="_blank" >filed</a> in April, is still <a class="Link" href="https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/73192632/tan-v-city-of-san-jose/" target="_blank" >pending</a>. So are challenges to Flock cameras in cities such as <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/07/31/kansas-lawsuit-alprs-turn-a-license-plate-into-the-functional-equivalent-of-a-gps-tracking-device/" target="_blank" >Wichita</a>, Kansas, and <a class="Link" href="https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/72357963/lee-schmidt-v-city-of-norfolk/" target="_blank" >Norfolk</a>, Virginia.</p><p>Even when they reject such lawsuits, courts commonly <a class="Link" href="https://cases.justia.com/massachusetts/supreme-court/2020-sjc-12750.pdf?ts=1587124946" target="_blank" >acknowledge</a> that the legal picture <a class="Link" href="https://ij.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/Order-1-27-26.pdf" target="_blank" >could change</a> as the number and capabilities of license plate readers multiply. If so, it seems likely that Hill will eventually be joined by other judges who recognize the perils of "indiscriminate mass surveillance."</p><p><i>Jacob Sullum is a senior editor at Reason magazine.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-f80000" name="module-f80000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Lobbyist campaign cash helps fuel Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton's run for U.S. Senate seat
entries.summary: <p>As she vies to replace retiring U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton is accepting a number of campaign contributions from lobbyists representing special interests, records show.</p><p>Some of the lobbyists work for firms that lobby Illinois’ state government, overseen by her political ally and benefactor, Gov. JB Pritzker. Others work for firms that lobby Congress and other arms of the federal government.</p><p>Much of that money has come since Stratton was endorsed by the campaign reform organization End Citizens United last November after the organization lauded Stratton for “refusing corporate PAC donations and pledging to crack down on dark money in politics.”</p><p>The motivations for the lobbyist donations to Stratton, a Democrat facing off against Republican Don Tracy in the Nov. 3 general election, were not always clear. But the lobbyists or their firms represent clients at the state and federal levels over subjects that include technology, education, energy and finance, records show.</p><p>Tracy has gotten just a fraction of the contributions Stratton has received — overall, and from lobbyists, according to an analysis of the Don Tracy for Illinois account.</p><p>John Millner, a lobbyist for Cook County Board President Toni Preckwinkle’s office, as well as several police groups, gave Tracy’s campaign fund $260 earlier this year, according to Federal Election Commission records. A Carol Stream resident, Millner is a former cop and legislator.</p><p>The Stratton donors include employees of Mercury Public Affairs, a bi-partisan firm that helps clients with everything from crisis management and political consulting to “grassroots coalition building” and lobbying, according to its web site.</p><p>The company includes former U.S. Rep. Cheri Bustos (D-Ill.). President Donald Trump’s chief of staff Susie Wiles, a Republican, was once a Mercury leader.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-040000" name="image-040000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3f14909/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4832x2712+0+256/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fa0%2F7e%2F9bb7e9374a72ac30f08a32340f80%2Fgovernorsday-081425-35.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f696e77/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4832x2712+0+256/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fa0%2F7e%2F9bb7e9374a72ac30f08a32340f80%2Fgovernorsday-081425-35.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/71bb49f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4832x2712+0+256/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fa0%2F7e%2F9bb7e9374a72ac30f08a32340f80%2Fgovernorsday-081425-35.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Former U.S. Rep. entries.title: Democrat Patty García faces Chris Getty, two other challengers in race for Rep. 'Chuy' García's seat
entries.summary: <p>The congressional race for the seat left vacant by U.S. Rep. Jesus “Chuy” García's<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2025/11/03/jesus-chuy-garcia-reelection-dropping-out-chief-of-staff-running" > surprise last-minute resignation</a> has seen its fair share of drama.</p><p>It began with outcries over the congressman’s ballot switcheroo — with Chuy García's then-chief of staff Patty García quickly gathering signatures to run. Then independent candidates Ald. Byron Sigcho-Lopez and Mayra Macías lobbed anti-democratic allegations after being <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/07/21/byron-sigcho-lopez-mayra-macias-chuy-garcia-congressional-seat-independent-candidates-ballot-removal" >tossed from the ballot </a>for failing to submit the minimum number of valid petition signatures required to run as independents. </p><p>Now, as the dust settles before the Nov. 3 election, just four candidates remain: Patty García, Lyons Mayor Chris Getty, who's running as an independent, Republican candidate Lupe Castillo and Working Class Party candidate Ed Hershey.</p><h3>Moving past the primary </h3><p>Patty García has been running full force since the primary, including racking up more than 175 endorsements from Democrats, including U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Lt. Gov Juliana Stratton and Rep. Delia Ramirez. She's also backed by the Illinois AFL-CIO, Chicago Federation of Labor and SEIU Illinois State Council. She says she’s focusing on immigration and affordability, with many people in the district still fearful of ICE enforcement and reluctant to apply for citizenship. She said she's surpassed more than $420,000 in fundraising. García had about $185,000 cash on hand at the end of June, according to the latest report filed with the Federal Election Commission. </p><p>She’s consistently said that voters aren’t focusing on the “process” in which she got on the ballot. In announcing her run in November, she also defended it, saying any other Democrat could have jumped into the race before Rep. García opted out.</p><p>She’s also trying to gain the support of voters who planned to support either Sigcho-Lopez or Macías.</p><p>“We’ve been trying to ensure that we’re connecting with people that may have supported them to ensure that we can bring them on and have a bigger picture here, a bigger tent, and making sure that we’re convening all groups,” Patty García said. “We’re trying to make sure that they know that we’re the best candidate, and that yes, they have a choice.”</p><p>With Patty García expected to get support from Chicago area Democrats in the district, she said she’s not concerned about Getty’s support in the district’s suburbs. The 4th district covers parts of the Southwest and Northwest sides of Chicago, as well as western suburbs like Lyons, La Grange and Riverside. </p><p>“No concern on my end,” Patty García said. “I will say that the majority of the mayors and the suburban leaders are with me. They know me, and they’ve worked with me. They trust me and I’ve been able to work with them as a chief of staff or district director.”</p><h3>Support beyond Chicago </h3><p>Getty, who has served as mayor of Lyons since 2009, said he’s confident he can go head to head with Patty García's campaign as the lone independent candidate.</p><p>“Our confidence level is very high, and that comes from one-on-one conversations on the ground with voters who want and desire an independent,” Getty said. “The number one question I get is, ‘Democrat or Republican?’ And I proudly say independent and everybody’s response by and large is, ‘I love that.’”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/10/31/lyons-mayor-chris-getty-campaign-loan-federal-tax-lien-state-elections-board" >Getty said </a>he’s focusing on uniting voters and letting them know he’s not running on a partisan divide. He’s hearing voters’ concerns over the cost of living and said members of Congress must find a way to provide relief. </p><p>“They’re not going to have a silver bullet to address cost of living, but I think we as elected representatives have to do whatever we can to assess every single vote," Getty said. "How is this going to affect working families? Is it going to make it harder? Is it going to make it easier for everyday life?”</p><p></p><p></p><p>He said he’s not just banking on support from the suburbs.</p><p>“One would think, ‘Hey Chris, don’t spend your time over there. Just stay in the suburbs,’” Getty said. “No, we’re going everywhere and the reception is exceptionally positive.”</p><h3>Other options for voters</h3><p>Ed Hershey has been teaching at Lindblom Math and Science Academy in West Englewood for 16 years and says his work in schools has shown him how a lack of resources can affect students. He’s also served as a union representative and ran for alderman of the 25th Ward in 2015.</p><p>“By running, I can give voice to that idea that we, working people, need to press for our own interests,” Hershey has said of his campaign.</p><p>Castillo, a Republican, says she’s running on a platform of “pro-family values and policies." She says she’s the only candidate that “will protect women’s sports and girl’s bathrooms,” and who would support law enforcement over criminals. She’s also supportive of voter ID and school choice.</p>

entries.title: MCA chief Madeleine Grynsztejn wanted to close the museum gender gap. She hopes the work will continue.
entries.summary: <p>Madeleine Grynsztejn can point to many successes as she looks back on her 18-year tenure atop the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago. But perhaps her most far-reaching achievement has been pledging that 50% of all artists featured in exhibitions, acquisitions and programming identify as women.</p><p>The museum announced its tenure,<b> </b>believes the MCA is the only art museum in the country to make such a commitment. The museum did so, she notes, before the #MeToo movement gained force in 2017, and before the Time’s Up group founded by Hollywood celebrities a year later began raising money for victims of sexual harassment.</p><p>“This is not woke,” she said. “This is fairness. This is equity. This is serving our public. We are a public trust, and our public is 50-plus % female.”</p><p>Who will succeed Grynsztejn and carry the effort forward<b> </b>at the MCA<b> </b>is the subject of much speculation in art circles. During her tenure, which has at times been controversial, Grynsztejn has constantly worked to stretch the notion of what an art museum can be with a motto of being “artist activated and audience engaged in equal measure.”</p><p>That’s an important motto for the MCA, which is not Chicago’s largest art destination but has continued – under her leadership – its longtime “first of firsts” practice of seeking out new artistic talents and being the first museum to showcase them.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure Grynsztejn, the MCA announced last week the creation of the Madeleine Fund for Women Artists, which will be funded by a $5 million donation from board member Leslie Bluhm on behalf of her family. As its name suggests, it will provide support for the collection and exhibition of works by women artists.</p><p>Throughout her time at the MCA, Grynsztejn has pushed to spotlight worthy Chicago artists while also ensuring that the museum remains globally relevant. She says she has also put diversity at the forefront of all it has done from hiring curators to making acquisitions. Later this fall, the MCA will showcase a major exhibition featuring the work of Rashid Johnson, an alum of Columbia College and the School of the Art Institute whose work is among those <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts/2026/07/09/art-is-all-around-you-at-the-obama-presidential-center" target="_blank" ><u>commissioned </u></a>by the new Obama Presidential Center. It will devote another in 2027 to <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts/2026/08/07/other-washingtons-amanda-williams-public-art-project-monument-george" target="_blank" ><u>Amanda Williams,</u></a> a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/10/12/23398990/macarthur-fellows-genius-grants-2022-reuben-jonathan-miller-tomeka-reid-amanda-williams" target="_blank" ><u>MacArthur Foundation “genius grant” winner</u></a> based in the Bridgeport neighborhood who blurs the boundaries of art and architecture.</p><p>Naomi Beckwith, deputy director and chief curator at the Guggenheim Museum in New York, called Grynsztejn’s nearly two decades as the MCA’s director a “seismic shift” in the institution’s trajectory.</p><p>“It’s a very, very different institution than the one she inherited, and I would say an unqualifiedly better one, with all respect to her predecessors,” said Beckwith, who spent 10 years at the MCA, leaving in 2021 as a senior curator.</p><div blooming collection </b></h3><p>Grynsztejn, 64, announced earlier this year that she will step down at the end of 2026, right before the MCA marks its 60th anniversary next year. In 1967, the museum was founded in a small building at 237 E. Ontario. Two years later, it became the first structure to be wrapped by Christo and Jean-Claude, who became known for their controversial large-scale environmental projects like partitioning a mountain valley near Rifle, Colo., with a 1,250-foot-wide orange curtain.</p><p>The MCA began collecting art in 1974 – its first acquisition was a piece by famed pop artist Marisol Escobar – and moved in 1996 into its present location, a five-story building in Streeterville designed by Berlin architect Josef Paul Kleihues.</p><p>Grynsztejn said she decided this year was the right moment for her to move on to the next chapter in her professional life in which she wants to find new ways to support artists outside the confines of a museum.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div Here, the interior of the museum is pictured in 1972.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Chicago Sun-Times Negative Collection</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>She was born in Lima, Peru, and grew up in Caracas, Venezuela. She got her start as an associate curator at the Museum of Contemporary Art, San Diego, in 1986, and after two other positions, became senior curator of painting and sculpture at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art in 2000.</p><p>She got to know Chicago in the early 1990s, when she served as associate curator of 20th century painting and sculpture at the Art Institute of Chicago, organizing such shows as “Affinities: Chuck Close and Tom Friedman” (1996) and “About Place: Recent Art of the Americas” (1995).</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/art/2026/01/29/art-institute-chicago-president-james-rondeau" target="_blank" ><u>James Rondeau,</u></a> now president and director of the Art Institute, succeeded her in 1998, and he praised her short stay in what he called an “underdog job” because contemporary art held little sway there at the time. He complimented “About Place” and noted that she was the first person to bring a work by now-celebrated Chicago artist Kerry James Marshall into that museum’s collection.</p><p>He called Grynsztejn a “brilliant curator,” and he believes she has led the MCA with what he called “curatorial-centered values,” including diligently supporting artists.</p><p>She has continued what she calls the museum’s longtime practice of seeking out new artistic talents and being the first museum to showcase them. Artists trust us,” Grynsztejn said.</p><p>But the director’s tenure has not been without its challenges. In 2021, as cultural institutions grappled with the COVID-19 pandemic and its impact on audiences, a group of artists withdrew their work from an exhibition titled “The Long Dream” to protest the layoffs of more than 40 workers a few months earlier.</p><p>In June of that year, a group of visitor-services and other employees formed a group called MCAccountable, to lobby the museum for change, including greater transparency around work pay and benefits.</p><p>“Artists demanded, along with staff and community, that the museum not only be excellent in its exhibitions and programs but it also be excellent in its operations, that it be as ethical on the inside as the messages it was putting on the walls.” Grynsztejn said, “And that came down to paying people well.”</p><p>The director called the COVID-19 shutdown and labor unrest the most difficult moments of her career. “The circumstances brought me to my knees,” she said. And a year later, the museum <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2024/03/22/mca-worker-union-museum-of-contemporary-art-afscme" target="_blank" ><u>voluntarily recognized</u></a> the MCA Workers United, which represents more than 70 workers at the institution.</p><p>In March, the union reached a four-year agreement with the museum that raises wages by 12% across the board, with a 3% increase retroactive to July 1, 2025. “As director, Madeleine Grynsztejn respected the right of employees to form a union, voluntarily recognizing MCA Workers United/AFSCME, and we were able to reach agreement on a fair first contract,” Anders Lindall, a spokesman for AFSCME Council 31, said in an e-mailed statement.</p><h3><b>The art of balancing museum budgets</b></h3><p>One thing Grynsztejn can take credit for is helping the MCA find more steady financial footing. The years post-COVID-19 brought budget deficits ($6.7 million in fiscal year 2022-23 and $2.3 million in fiscal year 2023-24, according to its most recent annual reports) and, like many cultural institutions, mounting expenses.</p><p>But the institution has weathered tough economics, reporting a<b> </b>$200,000 surplus in fiscal year 2024-25. “We are financially viable here,” Grynsztejn said, “but that is not to say that we haven’t been challenged as every other institution has been since COVID to make sure to balance revenue with expenses.”</p><p>It helps that the museum’s endowment has grown from $55.7 million when the director first arrived to $157.2 million as of Aug. 31, according to figures provided by the director. The 2025 annual report shows that investment earnings from that endowment provided 21% of the museum’s revenue in fiscal year 2024-25.</p><p>In all, Grynsztejn takes credit for raising more than $300 million in donations during her tenure, including an $82 million campaign in advance of the MCA’s 50th anniversary in 2017 that included $16 million for an interior facelift meant to make the museum more welcoming. The project converted 12,000 square feet into Marisol, a James Beard-recognized restaurant, education wing and public gathering space known as the Commons.</p><p>Among the most visible aspects of what any art museum does are its exhibitions, and Grynstztejn has overseen a mix of blockbusters as well as less-flashy, probing shows like the Doris Salcedo retrospective in 2015 – the Colombian artist’s first such in-depth survey anywhere.</p><p>“I think Madeleine will be remembered for a program that tries to balance real intellectual concerns with a sense of pop,” Beckwith said. “Madeleine was not someone who was afraid of a little bit of spectacle.”</p><p>The Salcedo show offered a cross-section of her haunting sculptures and installations that recall and mourn the thousands of lives lost to Mellon Foundation to develop a Latinx and Caribbean art initiative focused on the exhibitions and acquisitions of work from those regions and help fund its transition to a completely bilingual Spanish/English museum.</p><p>This bilingual approach is “smart business,” said the director, who speaks Spanish and French, because nearly 30 percent of Chicago’s population is Latino. Since the change to bilingual signage and labels, attendance at the museum’s monthly free family days has doubled, with much of the increase coming from Spanish-speaking visitors.</p><h3><b>What’s next at the MCA</b></h3><p>Who will succeed Grynsztejn is the subject of current chatter, with the word around the Chicago art scene that Beckwith could be it. The museum has said nothing about who will fill the soon-to-vacant position. Beckwith will only say she is “busy for quite some time,” an apparent reference to her serving as the artistic director of Documenta 16, an international art fair set to take place in Germany June 12-Sept. 19, 2027.</p><p>“I don’t remember Chicago being so gossipy,” Beckwith said with a laugh when asked if she is in the running for the position.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ac0000" name="image-ac0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4894666/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2571x1443+0+1079/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb5%2Fd5%2F35c5757742b29bd100fd037f9e83%2Fgettyimages-1795863025.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0a0dddb/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2571x1443+0+1079/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb5%2Fd5%2F35c5757742b29bd100fd037f9e83%2Fgettyimages-1795863025.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6499a9c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2571x1443+0+1079/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb5%2Fd5%2F35c5757742b29bd100fd037f9e83%2Fgettyimages-1795863025.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Naomi Beckwith attends the 2023 Guggenheim International Gala at Solomon R. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6499a9c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2571x1443+0+1079/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb5%2Fd5%2F35c5757742b29bd100fd037f9e83%2Fgettyimages-1795863025.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/735b75d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2571x1443+0+1079/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb5%2Fd5%2F35c5757742b29bd100fd037f9e83%2Fgettyimages-1795863025.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6499a9c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2571x1443+0+1079/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb5%2Fd5%2F35c5757742b29bd100fd037f9e83%2Fgettyimages-1795863025.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Who will succeed Grynsztejn is the subject of current chatter, with the word around the Chicago art scene that Beckwith could be it. “I don’t remember Chicago being so gossipy,” Beckwith said with a laugh when asked if she is in the running for the position. Here, she attends the 2023 Guggenheim International Gala.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Craig Barritt/Getty Images for Guggenheim Museum</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>There are plenty of notions of what the new director should be like. Beckwith called for someone with the same “dynamic spirit” as Grynsztejn. Rondeau would like a continuation of the artist-centered values described earlier. Cave, who joined the board in 2025 as artist trustee, hopes to see someone with “fire” and who is fearless and is focused on the future.</p><p>“It’s a tough museum,” Pope said. “It’s not big. It’s not small. I think it’s going to take someone who is able to see both the small picture and the big picture. It’s a place that is on the big map in the art world, and it wants to stay relevant there and, at the same time, it wants to stay relevant to a very specific Chicago community.”</p><p>As she looks forward, Grynsztejn believes the MCA and her successor must embrace and respond to the next generation of artists, philanthropists and audience members and their evolving needs and wants.</p><p>“We need bold leadership on all fronts,” she said. “The greatest challenges to museums are the greatest challenges to society at large. Museums build citizenship muscles. We need to build citizenship muscle as a society. Museums are places where all or our welcome. We need all to be welcome as a society and be less divisive. So we’re the antidote to the challenges.”</p>

entries.title: Lookalike tan suit Barack Obama wore on Larry David's HBO show is missing
entries.summary: <p>SANTA MONICA, Calif. – The controversial tan suit former President Barack Obama wore to a 2014 press conference? He gave it away years ago, so it’s not in Chicago’s newly opened Obama museum. The dead-ringer tan suit Obama wore in a hilarious HBO comedy sketch with Larry David? For now, that can’t be located either.</p><p>This doesn’t mean the replica is lost or stolen. The lookalike suit, rented for $300 to $400 a week, may simply be sitting somewhere in the vast costume department at Warner Bros. Studio in nearby Burbank. I had to cancel a visit to photograph the stand-in suit after it could not be found.</p><p>Last December, the HBO show “Life, Larry and the Pursuit of Unhappiness: An Almost History of America” returned the replica to the costume shop after taping with Obama in secret. The skit — filmed on a soundstage near Los Angeles where Obama’s Oval Office was recreated in exquisite detail — debuted in August, in the series finale.</p><p>More sleuthing has to be done to find that suit. This is an unfolding story.</p><p>I’m now in pursuit of two Obama tan suits: the real suit and the stand-in.</p><p>The shtick in the HBO show was based on a very funny but totally untrue story about how Obama ended up in that tan suit at an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/08/27/emmett-till-dr-martin-luther-king-jr-mlk-barack-obama-tavis-smiley-pursuit-tan-suit" target="_blank" ><u>Aug. 28, 2014, press conference</u></a> in the White House briefing room. In an outsized political backlash, right-wing and Republican critics of the nation’s first Black president accused him of looking unpresidential. The controversy raised questions about racial double standards, since other presidents had worn tan suits without reproach.</p><p>In the HBO version, this was comedian Larry David’s fault.</p><p>David plays an obnoxious presidential aide who spills a Mango Tango smoothie on a navy blue suit Obama intends to wear. To cover up his misdeed, David talks the president into wearing a tan suit instead because it’s “Casual Friday.” The suit just happens to be around the Oval Office because Obama is making his clothing choices for a NATO summit in Italy.</p><p>As Obama heads to the press conference in the tan suit, he asks David, “You sure about this?”</p><p>“I’ve never been more sure about anything in my life,” David says. “People are going to be talking about this for a long, long, time.”</p><p>We’re all in on the gag. That Obama’s 2014 attackers tried to create a scandal over a mere clothing choice — well, in 2026 that says far more about them than him. Given the ongoing grift and graft coming out of President Donald Trump and his administration, the 2014 attempts to make a scandal out of a tan suit look ridiculous.</p><div class="Enhancement" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Former President Barack Obama wears a replica tan suit for a skit on Larry’s David’s HBO show “Life, Larry, And The Pursuit Of Unhappiness.”</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>John Johnson/HBO</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The idea for the skit came from Los Angeles-based Higher Ground Productions, founded in 2018 by Obama and former first lady Michelle. The Obamas and Ethan Lewis, Higher Ground’s head of non-fiction and sports are among the executive producers.</p><p>Lewis told me “the tan suit was one that we knew we wanted to unpack” when they were brainstorming an Obama-David spoof segment in the spring of 2025.</p><p>“You know, presidential scandals are so serious these days, let’s revisit one that’s a little more lighthearted, right?” Lewis said.</p><p>Jeff Schaffer, the show’s co-creator, director and an executive producer, told me: “Ethan came to us and said President Obama’s interested in doing something on the tan suit. What if it was Larry’s fault?” he recalled. “I think, to be honest, we were surprised and so excited at how game the president was to do this. So, we’re like, ‘Oh, we’re going to take this gift.’”</p><p>The big question for Christina Mongini, the show’s costume designer, was whether Obama still had the original tan suit.</p><p>Lewis said he asked Joe Paulsen, the head of business and strategy for Higher Ground.</p><p>Paulsen told Lewis, “I think it’s been given away … [It’s] probably in a thrift store somewhere.”</p><p>With no hope of quickly tracking down the original, Mongini told me, “I’m sort of used to the hunt.”</p><p>Obama’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/09/05/anatomy-barack-obamas-tan-suit" target="_blank" ><u>custom, hand-stitched suit</u></a> was made by the late Brooklyn tailor <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/09/05/holocaust-survivor-tailor-barack-obama-tan-suit-martin-greenfield-clothiers" target="_blank" ><u>Martin Greenfield</u></a>, a Holocaust survivor who sewed his first stitches as a teen at the Auschwitz Nazi concentration camp during World War II. For the HBO skit, Mongini needed a traditional two-button suit with a notched lapel about 3 ¼ inches wide. The jacket had flap pockets and side vents.</p><p>Mongini’s team contacted Greenfield Clothiers in Brooklyn, New York. Because of the extreme confidentiality surrounding the show, Mongini’s team could not just order a duplicate — or get many details.</p><p>“We couldn’t tell anybody while we were looking for this suit why we were looking for it,” Mongini said. “I thought we could find some options. We didn’t.”</p><p>Time was running out. Mongini turned to the Warner Bros. costume rental house. “I’m flipping through the suits at Warner Bros. and this [one] just sort of jumped out at me, and I could tell it was a beautifully made suit and the weight of the wool was really fine,” she said.</p><p>“I found one suit — one suit in Los Angeles, one suit at Warner Bros., and it didn’t even have a label. It was in the Gold Room, and I remember being in there thinking, ‘This looks so beautiful, and it’s close to his size,’” Mongini said. “[This was] literally our only option.”</p><p>When they did the fitting at the Higher Ground office, Obama examined the suit on the rack. Mongini recalled the former president saying it looked and felt like the original.</p><p>“And I just felt, you know, what luck … because I knew he had to walk in and it had to … feel right,” she said. “His instant response was yes.”</p><p>Mongini said she’s “still overwhelmed by the fact that we took one suit to a fitting and it worked.”</p><p>And now that suit is AWOL too.</p><p>Even so, Mongini is optimistic the show suit was just misplaced and can be found. She does not suspect anything nefarious.</p><p>Presidential historian Colleen Shogan served as the Archivist of the United States during the Biden administration, leading the National Archives and Records Administration. She said the original suit has enormous historic value — and the ringer suit is significant too, since the former president wore it in the comedy take of a presidential moment.</p><p>If the HBO suit surfaces, it would be worthwhile for the Obama Museum to acquire it, she added.</p><p>Said Shogan, “If I was a curator at the Obama Presidential Museum, it sure would be an interesting item for the collection.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-070000" name="module-070000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Pursuit of the Suit</h3><br>On Aug. 28, 2014, the tan suit that then-President Barack Obama wore to a White House press conference became an unexpected story. After his presidency, Obama reportedly gave the suit away cleaning out his closet. Follow as former Sun-Times Washington Bureau Chief <b>Lynn Sweet</b> hunts down the original tan suit — and what makes it so compelling along the way. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/tansuit" target="_blank" >suntimes.com/tansuit</a><br><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-dddea0e2-a259-11f1-9f97-593067e43792"><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/08/17/hunt-for-barack-obamas-tan-suit-help-us-find-it" target="_blank" ><b>We’re on the hunt for Barack Obama’s tan suit. Help us find it.</b></a></li><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/08/27/emmett-till-dr-martin-luther-king-jr-mlk-barack-obama-tavis-smiley-pursuit-tan-suit" ><b>Emmett Till, Dr. King, Obama and Aug. 28</b></a></li><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/09/05/holocaust-survivor-tailor-barack-obama-tan-suit-martin-greenfield-clothiers" ><b>The remarkable story of the Holocaust survivor who made Barack Obama’s tan suit</b></a></li><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/09/05/anatomy-barack-obamas-tan-suit" ><b>The anatomy of Barack Obama’s tan suit</b></a></li></ul></div> </div><p><b><i>Contact us</i></b><i>: Please join us on this journey by sending tips, story ideas or suggestions on who to interview. Email: <u>tansuit@suntimes.com</u>.</i></p>

entries.title: Chicago woman riding motorcycle crashes and is killed on Kennedy Expressway's Ontario Street feeder ramp downtown
entries.summary: <p>A Northwest Side woman was killed when the motorcycle she was driving hit a concrete wall Wednesday afternoon on the Kennedy Expressway's Ontario Street feeder ramp. </p><p>Kaitlin Rose Wagner Zbonski, 29, struck a concrete wall and went over the wall, landing in the southbound lanes just before 3 p.m., the Illinois State Police said.</p><p>Zbonski was pronounced dead shortly before 4 p.m. at Stroger Hospital, according to the Cook County medical examiner's office. </p><p>Several lanes shut down by the crash were reopened around 6 p.m. </p>

Dick Durbin (D-Ill.)</a>, Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton is accepting a number of campaign contributions from lobbyists representing special interests, records show. In total, Stratton has raised more than $5 million since the beginning of last year, while her opponent, Republican Don Tracy, has reported less than $400,000.</p><p><b>The sources</b>: Some of the lobbyists work for firms that lobby Illinois' state government, overseen by her political ally and benefactor, Gov. that money has come since Stratton was endorsed last November by the campaign reform organization End Citizens United after the group lauded Stratton for "refusing corporate PAC donations and pledging A police report <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydtujuyk-l-c/" target="_blank" >first obtained by the Sun-Times</a> showed a woman reported being assaulted early Sunday at the frat house.</p><p><b>Safety in spotlight</b>: Alpha Epsilon Pi isn't officially recognized by UChicago, and the people involved weren't students.
