entries.title: Johnson's veto of bid to curtail his borrowing power survives override try — by one vote
entries.summary: <p>After an emotional and racially charged debate, Mayor Brandon Johnson’s fourth veto survived an attempted override Wednesday, preventing the City Council from making it more difficult to issue city debt by raising the threshold for approval from 26 votes to 30 votes.</p><p> Retiring Ald. Marty Quinn (13th), who championed the reform, fell one vote short of the 34 votes he needed to thwart the mayor’s veto. The final vote was 33 to 17, allowing Johnson to avoid what would have been a humiliating defeat by the slimmest of margins.</p><p>“There’s no secret that there are a number of members of City Council still adjusting to a progressive agenda,” the mayor said at his post-Council meeting news conference.</p><p>“Last I checked, 26 votes is still a majority, and that still exists.”</p><p> </p><p>Prior to the vote, Budget Committee Chair Jason Ervin (28th) had delivered an impassioned speech, accusing his colleagues of targeting Johnson because he is Black.</p><p>His voice rising, Ervin asked his colleagues, “Who gives away power?... Nobody gives away power and I didn’t come down here to give up mine.”</p><p></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-930000" name="image-930000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5d7b1a8/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F16%2Fe7%2Fb6b9136445d7ba331608b1427611%2Fcitycouncil-261015-39.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e31b268/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F16%2Fe7%2Fb6b9136445d7ba331608b1427611%2Fcitycouncil-261015-39.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c898260/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F16%2Fe7%2Fb6b9136445d7ba331608b1427611%2Fcitycouncil-261015-39.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Ald. Jason Ervin (28th) at a Chicago City Council meeting on Oct. 14, 2026. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c898260/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F16%2Fe7%2Fb6b9136445d7ba331608b1427611%2Fcitycouncil-261015-39.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/fe2ff7c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F16%2Fe7%2Fb6b9136445d7ba331608b1427611%2Fcitycouncil-261015-39.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c898260/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F16%2Fe7%2Fb6b9136445d7ba331608b1427611%2Fcitycouncil-261015-39.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Ald. Jason Ervin (28th), shown during Wednesday’s Chicago City Council meeting, opposed efforts to override Mayor Brandon Johnson’s veto of a measure intended to make it harder for the city to borrow money. The ordinance would have required a three-fifths vote of the Council, not just a simple majority, to approve such borrowing.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“Why do the rules need to change?" Ervin continued. "You want to call it independence. [But] it’s ironic that we only talk about independence and executive oversight when the person sitting up there looks like me.” </p><p>“It happened under [Harold] Washington. It happened for about 15 minutes under Lori Lightfoot and it’s been going pretty much all the term under Johnson. Three Black mayors. And all of the sudden the rules.. become an issue. Call it independence. You want to call it reform. You want to call it checks and balances. But again, where was that concern before under Daley, under Emanuel …" </p><p>North Side Ald. Maria Hadden (49th) stuck with the mayor, saying she still “drives around the city and sees huge swaths of the city that have been neglected and just tossed aside.”</p><p>Hadden called Quinn's proposal "a distraction," but at the same time, she warned Johnson his own failure to collaborate with the Council had all but invited alderpersons to push back.</p><p>"We wouldn’t be here having this conversation and you having to have a veto if we had better relations with Council and your office," Hadden told Johnson. “We need the fifth floor — we need you and your team — to hear these concerns." </p><p></p><p>Downtown Ald. Bill Conway (34th), a former investment banker who teaches college finance, said the notion that requiring 30 votes instead of 26 votes “will somehow delay infrastructure investment simply doesn’t square with the facts.”</p><p>“This is about the difference between borrowing to build our city’ s future and mortgaging the city’s future,” Conway said. “Our predatory borrowing of money has pushed obligations onto future generations. We are those future generations, and the bills are coming due.”</p><p>It’s the second time Quinn has tried and failed to override a Johnson veto. The first time, the mayor vetoed a citywide ban on hemp products that Quinn championed. Though he failed again, Quinn said he made his point about the danger of borrowing more money and, increasingly, structuring the repayment schedule to postpone the day of reckoning.</p><p>Last year, the Council almost blocked an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/02/18/830-million-bond-issue-city-borrowing-costs-backloaded-repayment-schedule" target="_blank" >$830 million general obligation bond issue</a> that included a back-loaded repayment schedule raising the overall price tag to $2 billion.</p><p>“This has been a really good fight on behalf of the taxpayers of Chicago. We’ve had some really good conversations about the city’s debt. You couple that with our pension obligations, that’s 40% of our operating budget. That’s real. It’s not gonna change,” Quinn said.</p><p>West Side Ald. Emma Mitts (37th) supported the override despite what she claimed were unspecified threats to withhold money for people in her ward affected by devastating flooding in 2023.</p><p>Without naming names, Mitts said she had been approached by “bullies” who warned her that, “If you don’t vote on this, you won’t get that.”</p><p>“One thing that I’m very passionate about is you messing with my community,” Mitts said.</p><h3>Other action at Wednesday’s meeting</h3><p>The Council also agreed to expand citywide a so-called “Smart Streets” program using <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/10/09/chicago-smart-streets-bus-bike-lane-violation" >surveillance cameras on CTA buses</a> and Chicago Department of Transportation vehicles to catch motorists parking in bus and bike lanes and provide photo evidence of those violations for automatic ticketing. The pilot program, confined mostly to downtown areas, has so far generated $4.5 million in parking fines. </p><p>Alderpersons also confirmed new members for the Board of Ethics, as well two new members of Johnson’s cabinet: Fleet and Facilities Management Commissioner JuanPablo Prieto and Human Resources Commissioner Tiheta Hinton.</p><p>During Tuesday’s confirmation hearing, Prieto promised to cut skyrocketing vehicle and fuel costs by reducing the number of vehicles permanently assigned to city employees and forcing more employees to use pool cars instead. </p><p>Johnson’s appointment of Renee Hatcher, daughter of former Gary, Ind. Mayor Richard Hatcher, to succeed Mary Richardson-Lowry as corporation counsel was pulled amid complaints that Hatcher lacks the experience needed for the job. Also, the Council voted down Johnson's appointments to Chicago Housing Authority board seats. Some Council members have seen Johnson's proposed CHA appointments as his attempt to get rid of the agency's executive director, Keith Pettigrew.</p><p></p><p></p><p></p>

entries.title: Man who caused shutdown at Chicago's federal courthouse pleads guilty, faces 2 years in prison
entries.summary: <p>The man who caused the lockdown, evacuation and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2025/07/22/emergency-ongoing-at-dirksen-federal-building-in-loop" target="_blank" >hourslong standoff</a> at the Dirksen Federal Courthouse last year pleaded guilty Thursday<b> </b>to<b> </b>possessing<b> </b>a dangerous weapon<b> </b>in a federal court facility and now faces up to two years in prison.</p><p>U.S. District Judge Mary<b> </b>Rowland<b> </b>set<b> </b>Mario<b> </b>Santoyo’s sentencing<b> </b>for<b> </b>Jan. 12. Santoyo admitted to the judge<b> </b>that he’d carried<b> </b>a knife<b> </b>with a blade<b> </b>longer than 2 ½ inches<b> </b>into Chicago’s federal<b> </b>courthouse<b> </b>in July 2025.</p><p>When a prosecutor briefly recounted the allegations against Santoyo, Rowland asked whether they were accurate.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2025/07/22/emergency-ongoing-at-dirksen-federal-building-in-loop" >Standoff at Dirksen Federal Courthouse with knife-wielding man ends after 9 hours</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>“That’s factual,” Santoyo told the judge.</p><p>Santoyo, 40, also wore a backpack<b> </b>the day of the courthouse lockdown. Authorities<b> </b>“had no idea”<b> </b>what was in it, his attorney<b> </b>has acknowledged.</p><p>The resulting standoff lasted roughly nine hours, shut down traffic on South Dearborn Street<b> </b>and eventually prompted an evacuation<b> </b>of the 30-story downtown tower.</p><p>Though Santoyo pleaded guilty to a crime that carries a maximum sentence of two years in prison, federal guidelines call for a sentence of no more than six months behind bars, authorities estimated Thursday.</p><p>When<b> </b>Santoyo<b> </b>arrived<b> </b>at the courthouse<b> </b>at 219 S. Dearborn<b> </b>around<b> </b>10:30 a.m. on July 22, 2025, he asked for the FBI and claimed that “gangsters”<b> </b>or<b> </b>"gangbanners"<b> </b>were trying to kill him, according to a criminal complaint.</p><p>After a court security officer<b> </b>told him<b> </b>the FBI’s offices<b> </b>were elsewhere<b> </b>and asked him to leave, Santoyo pulled out a knife, held it to his throat and said<b> </b>he was going to hurt himself, records show.</p><p>Occupants of the building in the floors above were notified by loudspeaker of the incident — and they were told to avoid the lobby. Authorities cleared Federal Plaza across the street, traffic on South Dearborn stopped flowing and a drone began to hover near the courthouse entrance.</p><p>Later, around 2 p.m., court officials told people in the building’s second-floor cafeteria how to safely exit the building. A short time later, they declared the evacuation mandatory. Officials led people through exits on the east side of the lobby, and then toward State Street.</p><p>Law enforcement officials could also be seen searching<b> </b>a silver<b> </b>Chevrolet<b> </b>Impala<b> </b>parked<b> </b>near<b> </b>West Jackson Street and South Dearborn.</p><p>It wasn’t until nearly 8 p.m. that law enforcement “used non-lethal force”<b> </b>and took Santoyo into custody, records show. He dropped the knife he’d been holding<b> </b>but turned out to be carrying a second blade, according to the feds.</p>

entries.title: From film icons to NBA stars, these celebrities are in town for the Chicago International Film Festival
entries.summary: <p>From Oscar nominees to NBA stars to “Iron Chef” icons, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/movies-and-tv/2026/09/17/chicago-international-film-festival-2026-lineup-carrie-coon-marlon-wayans" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago International Film Festival</u></a> is drawing an eclectic mix of celebrities to the city across the next two weeks.</p><p>A festival jury member this year, Chicago native <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2025/06/13/john-c-reilly-mr-romantic-steppenwolf-theatre-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>John C. Reilly</u></a> delighted crowds on the red carpet at Music Box Theatre, where the event series kicked off Wednesday night. He’s also in town to promote “<a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagofilmfestival.com/film/going-for-home/" target="_blank" ><u>Going For Home</u></a>,” a documentary he executive produced that is screening at the fest.</p><p>And tonight, Chicago Bulls veteran <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls/2026/01/24/night-to-remember-as-derrick-rose-bulls-jersey-retired" target="_blank" ><u>Derrick Rose</u></a> will appear at AMC Newcity 14 for a showing of “Three Colors: Pan-African,” a film he co-executive-produced with Steppenwolf Theatre Artistic Director Glenn Davis, and “Windfall” playwright <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/theater/2026/04/10/windfall-steppenwolf-play-tarell-alvin-mccraney-moonlight-writer" target="_blank" ><u>Tarell Alvin McCraney</u></a>. There’s a waitlist to see him present his new documentary, “<a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagofilmfestival.com/event/machupicchu/" target="_blank" ><u>Bob and David Climb Machu Picchu</u></a>,” at the festival. But fans can drive to Champaign to see him in his brother’s play, “<a class="Link" href="https://thevirginia.showare.com/eventperformances.asp?evt=1135" target="_blank" ><u>We Interrupt This Program</u></a>,” at The Virginia Theatre on Friday or Saturday.</p><p>As part of the 30th anniversary of the Black Perspectives program, Marlon Wayans will receive a Career Achievement Award and sit for a <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagofilmfestival.com/event/evening-with-marlon-wayans/" target="_blank" ><u>conversation</u></a> with actor <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/movies-and-tv/2026/08/26/moses-the-black-screening-chicago-melania-movie-alexandros-potter" target="_blank" ><u>Omar Epps</u></a>. href="https://www.chicagofilmfestival.com/film/once-upon-a-time-in-harlem/" target="_blank" ><u>Once Upon a Time in Harlem</u></a>,” one of the most anticipated documentaries this year.</p><div Tickets for select screenings and events are still available at <a class="Link" href="http://chicagofilmfestival.com" target="_blank" ><u>chicagofilmfestival.com</u></a>.</p>

entries.title: What's that dead zone in the 19th Ward?
entries.summary: <p><i>Editor’s note: This story first published on April 11, 2024. Mt. Greenwood Cemetery is now owned by Troost Cemeteries.</i></p><p>During the 2023 Chicago municipal elections, freelance journalist Taylor Moore often looked over the city’s ward and precinct maps. She noticed something unusual about the 19th Ward. This southwest ward that includes the Mt. Greenwood neighborhood had a rectangular cutout in the middle of the map. It turns out that hole is a cemetery. But there are many other cemeteries around the city that don’t show up as cutouts in the precinct maps. Press play to listen to the episode, and read the full story <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/curious-city/2024/04/11/mt-greenwood-cemetery-hole-in-the-19th-ward-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>here</u></a>.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-750000" name="html-embed-module-750000"></a><script async src="https://modules.wearehearken.com/wbez/embed/4190.js"></script> </div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Inspector general de CPS cierra caso de Hilario Domínguez con ningún ‘hallazgo accionable de conducta sexual inapropiada’
entries.summary: <p>La oficina del inspector general de las Escuelas Públicas de Chicago (CPS) cerró su investigación, que había reabierto recientemente, sobre las acusaciones de que el candidato a presidente de la junta escolar, Hilario Domínguez, tuvo una conducta inapropiada con una menor en 2017.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://hilarioforcps.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/oig-report_Redacted.pdf" target="_blank" >Según una carta enviada a Domínguez el miércoles</a> por la Oficina de Protección Estudiantil y Título IX de CPS, que Domínguez publicó en su sitio web de campaña, la oficina del inspector general “determinó que no hay un hallazgo accionable de conducta sexual inapropiada”.</p><p>La oficina no dio otros hallazgos sobre posibles infracciones de “políticas o pautas de CPS relacionadas con este incidente”. La carta señala que “la investigación ha concluido y el caso está cerrado” y que no se tomará ninguna otra medida.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-d80000" name="module-d80000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>La carta no es lo mismo que el informe del inspector general, que aún no se ha divulgado públicamente y que explicará por qué no hubo un hallazgo accionable.</p><p>La oficina del inspector general ya había determinado a comienzos de este año que las mismas acusaciones no estaban sustentadas, pero <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/10/13/investigacion-de-presunto-contacto-inapropiado-de-candidato-a-presidente-junta-de-cps-y-una-menor-podria-concluir" target="_blank" >recientemente decidió reabrir la investigación</a>. La mujer que hizo las acusaciones dijo que no fue entrevistada en la investigación original y que decidió dar la cara porque quería contar su historia.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://hilarioforcps.com/with-office-of-inspector-general-investigation-announcing-he-is-cleared-in-full-hilario-dominguez-recenters-race-on-competing-visions/" target="_blank" >En una publicación en el sitio web de campaña de Domínguez</a>, su abogada, Rima Kapitan, dijo que el informe del inspector general limpió el nombre de Domínguez de cualquier mala conducta.</p><p>La campaña de Domínguez también reiteró que las acusaciones provienen de Aída Flores, quien fue una de sus contrincantes en una carrera por un asiento en el Concejo Municipal en 2019. Flores es subdirectora de CPS y tiene vínculos personales con la joven que hizo las acusaciones, según varias fuentes.</p><p>“Los votantes que no estaban al tanto de la campaña de difamación de hace una década que difundió la campaña de Aída Flores cuando me postulé para concejal merecían una respuesta luego de que eso se sacara de nuevo este año”, escribió Domínguez <a class="Link" href="https://hilarioforcps.com/with-office-of-inspector-general-investigation-announcing-he-is-cleared-in-full-hilario-dominguez-recenters-race-on-competing-visions/" target="_blank" >en un comunicado</a>. “La OIG [Oficina del Inspector General] se las ha dado”.</p><p>Domínguez dijo que ahora quiere enfocar su campaña en los temas de educación “que les importan profundamente a los votantes”.</p><p>WBEZ se comunicó con la joven, que ahora tiene 26 años, a través de su abogado, quien no respondió de inmediato. Flores tampoco respondió de inmediato a una solicitud de comentarios.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Gun jammed when neo-Nazi tried to commit mass shooting at Hindu temple in Aurora, prosecutors say
entries.summary: <p>In a manifesto, Alexandros Paporakis identified as “a sociopathic white supremacist Neo Nazi filled with hatred, fantasizing about mass murder nearly every day,” according to court records.</p><p>Prosecutors say Paporakis, 19, spent two years planning a mass shooting and had been targeting a Hindu worship center in Aurora for two months.</p><p>But Sunday, when the day came to carry out the attack, Paporakis’ AR-style rifle jammed as Paporakis tried to shoot a man from a car, prosecutors said in a court proffer.</p><p>Paporakis sent messages to a co-worker at a Taco Bell in Arlington Heights, saying the man was “certainly saved by his God today,” prosecutors said.</p><p>That co-worker and another employee called 911, and Paporakis was found in the parking lot of a Palatine apartment complex, prosecutors said. A search of Paporakis’ apartment uncovered a rifle, bullet magazines, 300 rounds of ammunition and a gas can, as well as Nazi ephemera.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div with making a terrorist threat</a> and illegal gun possession, according to prosecutors. Paporakis was ordered detained during an initial court hearing Wednesday.</p><p>U.S. Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi said he and his family were at the temple when prosecutors say Paporakis attempted to carry out the attack.</p><p>“I am horrified that a white supremacist attempted to carry out a mass shooting targeting Indian Americans at the Hindu temple in Aurora where my family worships," Krishnamoorthi said in a statement.</p><p>Prosecutors detailed a series of warning signs and said Paporakis had become “manic” ahead of the planned attack, telling one co-worker that Sunday “was going to be a special day.” Paporakis texted another co-worker around 1:30 p.m. Sunday, saying the rifle had jammed and expressing an intent to “retry when I fix this,” prosecutors said.</p><p>Paporakis “regularly made disparaging comments … about people of other races particularly people from India,” prosecutors said. In the eight-page manifesto, Paporakis identified non-white people as “subhumans” and described a “plot to kill as many of them as possible,” according to prosecutors.</p><p>Associate Judge Andreana Turano noted that Paporakis was a self-described white supremacist in a detention order.</p><p><i>This is a developing story. entries.title: Riverside-Brookfield's Braeden Novak makes defenses pay with his running, passing
entries.summary: <p>Braeden Novak happens to like his given name, but the Riverside-Brookfield senior quarterback can’t deny the football fit of his nickname.</p><p>“Bubba,” he said. “My dad has been calling me that since I was a baby. Personally, I like my first name, but everybody calls me by my nickname. It’s like a bigger guy, it fits my personality.”</p><p>Novak indeed brings the attitude of a lineman to the quarterback position. He prefers passing to running, but Novak is also not afraid to put his head down and take the hit when he calls his own number.</p><p>“I do feel like I am able to break a lot of tackles,” Novak said. “I’ve been playing quarterback my whole life. You know you will get hit, getting hit is a part of football. I have to stay in and keep driving my legs to get the extra yards. Three extra yards can win you the game.”</p><p>Led by its dual-threat quarterback, Riverside-Brookfield (7-1) is riding a seven-game winning streak, the latest a 38-28 win over Glenbard East that clinched at least a share of the Upstate Eight East title.</p><p>Novak threw for 183 yards and ran for 133 in that game, including a 69-yard run on the third play. He’s thrown for 1,455 yards and 14 touchdowns with just two interceptions in eight games, He’s also the Bulldogs’ leading rusher with 559 yards and 11 TDs.</p><p>“What he is able to do both in the pass game and in the run game is special,” R-B coach Sam Styler said. “He’s a phenomenal leader that our guys rally around. He commands our offense in whatever role we need him to. His ability as a runner keeps a lot of defenses on their toes. When he throws, he’s able to locate and make great reads and progressions.”</p><p>Novak, also a standout baseball player, started playing football in the second or third grade. His dad, Jeff, who played football and baseball at Hinsdale South, coached him the first three years.</p><p>Novak shared the quarterback job last year with another junior, returning starter Giancarlo Garcia, in helping lead R-B to an 8-2 record, the program’s best season in almost a decade.<br>Novak took the starting job by Week 7 last year, with Garcia moving to running back. When Garcia did not return this season, Novak knew he’d have to bulk up with an increased running workload. He’s up to 200 pounds from 175 last year.</p><p>“People are relying on me a lot more, where last year it was the two of us,” Novak said. “This year the weight is on my back. I have to come through, I know the guys are trusting in me.”</p><p>R-B offensive coordinator Brad Vojcak told every ballcarrier before the season they’d have to get an extra 3 yards once they got hit.</p><p>It’s a message – not going down at first contact – that Novak took to heart, all the while making strong reads and setting up his blockers well.</p><p>“His vision sets him apart, what he is able to see with holes and just how hard he runs,” Styler said. “It’s rare to see a quarterback that likes to finish forward the way he does. He has embraced that. He is always finishing forward, always willing to take the extra yard. It speaks volumes of him as a leader that he is willing to take a hit and fall forward.”</p><p>Novak, whose older brother Ryan was a three-time all-conference player at R-B, doesn’t shy away from contact in games. Apparently he doesn’t mind getting his nose dirty in practice drills<br>either.</p><p>“Not at all. He doesn’t shy away from anything,” Styler said. “Any time we do a drill he takes on contact. He wants everything. He is not one that sits out drills tackling or running. We love that about him. He’s tough and durable, the total package.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.shawlocal.com/friday-night-drive/" target="_blank" >Read more high school football coverage a Friday Night Drive.</a></p>

entries.title: Bears picks: Week 6 at Falcons
entries.summary: <p>The Sun-Times' experts make their picks for Sunday's game in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/14/bears-falcons-coach-qb-michael-penix-in-line-to-start-ribs-injury-tua-tagovailoa-nfl" target="_blank" >Atlanta</a>:</p><h3>Patrick Finley</h3><p><b>Falcons, 24-21</b>: Are the Falcons good? Does it matter? If the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> play the way they did at Lambeau Field, the answer is no. <b>Season</b>: 2-3.</p><h3>Jason Lieser</h3><p><b>Bears, 30-26:</b> This is a tough game against an ascending Falcons team, but the Bears need it badly as the two participants from last season's Super Bowl await them next. <b>Season:</b> 2-3.</p><h3>Scoop Jackson</h3><p><b>Falcons, 35-30:</b> They always say don’t do anything when you are emotional. Because you lose rationality and you’ll regret what you did later. Whatever. Tried to no longer be mad about the Bears. It’s not working. <b>Season</b>: 2-3.</p><h3>Steve Greenberg</h3><p><b>Bears, 24-23:</b> The Bears have responded to the three worst games they’ve played under Ben Johnson — last year against Detroit and Baltimore, and this season against Minnesota — with wins. They’re also 12-2 outside the division since the start of last season. Somehow, some way, they get that “W.” <b>Season</b>: 3-2.</p><h3>Jeff Agrest</h3><p><b>Bears, 41-38:</b> With Caleb Williams and Michael Penix seemingly healthy — and no defense to speak of on either side — whoever has the ball last wins. I’m picking that team to be the Bears, who’ll win on a late, long field goal by Cairo Santos in Atlanta’s comfy indoor environs. <b>Season</b>: 1-4.</p>

entries.title: John Schriffen's absence from clincher might have clinched his fate with White Sox
entries.summary: <p>Where else would a Sox broadcaster have wanted to be on Sept. 24?</p><p>The team’s magic number to clinch its first playoff berth in five years was one. A September slog finally would wreap a reward with one more victory, and only the lowly Royals stood in the way. It had the makings of a momentous day.</p><p>For Sox TV voice John Schriffen, it would’ve been the capstone on a season that was a broadcaster’s dream, filled with home-run calls and dramatic finishes. Like Chicagoan and former NFL coach Marv Levy always said, “Where else would you rather be?”</p><p>To Schriffen, the answer was Las Vegas for a UFC Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu event.</p><p>Connor McKnight filled in alongside Steve Stone and did a fine job calling the clincher. But Schriffen’s absence had to touch a nerve with Sox brass. Even though he was contractually allowed to take a certain number of games off, did he have to take <i>that</i> game off?</p><p>With Schriffen’s three guaranteed years winding down and the chances of him returning seeming slim, perhaps being in the booth that day wouldn’t have mattered. But the Sox couldn’t have liked the optics of its TV voice choosing to be elsewhere than at a potential clincher.</p><p>If Schriffen wanted to return, missing that game couldn’t have helped. He declined to comment.</p><p>One of the reasons the Sox hired Schriffen before the 2024 season was his willingness to be available. That became a sticking point with his predecessor, Jason Benetti, who had expanded his profile nationally. Now, here was Schriffen, giving a side hustle priority.</p><p>And shouldn’t he have wanted to be there? After enduring one season with an MLB-record 121 losses and another with 102, this was a chance for Schriffen to celebrate something with the Sox. Criticize his broadcasting all you want — and I have — he earned that game.</p><p>I know what you’re thinking: Pick a lane, Agrest! <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports-media/2025/09/18/white-sox-john-schriffen-steve-stone-gordon-beckham-chicago-sports-network-mike-mccarthy-marquee-sports-network" >You wanted Schriffen fired after last season</a>, and now you’re complaining that he missed a game? What’s wrong with you?</p><p>To answer the second question first, plenty. The first question is fair, and I stand by that column. I would write most of it again today. As a baseball broadcaster, he’s not my cup of tea.</p><p>But while I filled in on the Sox beat this season, we got to know each other. Schriffen actually initiated it, approaching me in the team’s dugout before a game in Minnesota in June. I felt everyone in the dugout, mostly media, staring at us, waiting for a blowup.</p><p>It never happened.</p><p>It could have. He could’ve lit into me like a firework and made a scene that would’ve made Billy Martin blush. Instead, he simply reintroduced himself — we had talked before during Zoom and phone interviews — and started a conversation.</p><p>It opened a line of communication that hadn’t existed before and helped me understand him better. It didn’t change my opinion of his broadcasting, mind you, though his third season was his best.</p><p>He’s just not a baseball broadcaster. He didn’t have much experience before this job, and his style is more suited for the UFC than MLB. A longtime broadcaster told me that an announcer needs to give his voice somewhere to go. If you’re screaming for every home run, your voice has nowhere to go to indicate significance. The little homers blend with the big homers.</p><p>To me, it’s like Michael Buffer calling a baseball game. It’s all hype. But that’s what Schriffen likes. We agree to disagree.</p><p>Schriffen’s contract has an option for next season. If the Sox don’t pick it up, what will they do? That could depend on how much of a season there is next year, with a lockout looming. If it looks like Opening Day will be delayed significantly, they could hold off for a year on hiring someone and put someone already on the payroll in the booth. That likely would be McKnight.</p><p>If by some miracle it looks like much or all of the season will be played, there are plenty of good fits for the Sox, some with local ties. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports-media/2026/09/24/connor-onion-fox-sports-big-ten-network-mike-reis-robert-griffin-alexa-landestoy-southern-illinois-ball-state-lyons-township-la-grange-northwestern-indiana-college-football-chicago-bulls-adam-amin" >Connor Onion, a La Grange native and Chicago resident</a>, is a rising star in the industry. He calls baseball on Fox and FS1. Wayne Randazzo, a Berwyn native who also lives in Chicago, calls the Angels and Apple TV’s “Friday Night Baseball.”</p><p>The Sox also could scour the minor leagues for the next big name. Whatever they do, they need a baseball broadcaster. With a team on the rise, they need a TV booth to match. And before anyone gets any ideas, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports-media/2026/05/14/chicago-white-sox-radio-cubs-tv-len-kasper-harry-caray-ernie-harwell-jim-deshaies-darrin-jackson" >Len Kasper is not walking through that door</a>. He’s living his best life on the radio with Darrin Jackson. Besides, there’s no sense filling one spot and opening another.</p><p>And the way things look now, there probably will be a spot to fill in the Sox’ TV booth. If I could give candidates one piece of advice, it’d be this: tell the Sox that they’ll make sure to be at any and all potential clinchers, conflicts be damned.</p><h3>Remote patrol</h3><p>Northwestern’s football game at 11 a.m. Saturday at Michigan State will air on Peacock and NBC Sports Network. <b>Paul Burmeister</b> and analyst <b>Yogi Roth</b> have the call.</p><p>• Northern Illinois’ game at 2:30 p.m. Saturday at Wyoming will air on WGN 9. <b>Jack McMullen</b>, analyst <b>Cody Kessler</b> and reporter <b>Marshall Newhouse</b> will call it.</p><p>• <b>Kevin Burkhardt</b>, <b>Tom Brady</b>, <b>Erin Andrews</b> and <b>Tom Rinaldi</b> will call the Bears’ game at the Falcons at noon Sunday on Fox.</p>

entries.title: Juez detiene las operaciones de una planta que emite malos olores por demanda de la Ciudad y el Estado de Illinois
entries.summary: <p>Un juez ordenó la suspensión temporal de las operaciones de una planta de alimento para animales en el lado sureste de la ciudad, que durante años ha sido fuente de cientos de quejas por olores pútridos.</p><p>El juez Thomas Donnelly concedió una orden de restricción temporal a favor de la oficina del fiscal general de Illinois y de la Ciudad de Chicago, que <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/10/06/fiscal-general-y-ciudad-de-chicago-buscan-poner-fin-a-olores-repugnantes-de-una-planta-en-el-lado-sureste" target="_blank" >demandaron</a> a Pullman Innovations en agosto por los olores, alegando violaciones de las leyes estatales y municipales sobre la contaminación del aire.</p><p>La empresa fabrica un aditivo para alimento animal que usan agricultores que suministran huevos a la compañía alimentaria Dutch Farms.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-300000" name="module-300000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>En un comunicado emitido el miércoles, el fiscal general de Illinois, Kwame Raoul, dijo que la planta no debería reabrir hasta que “aborde los olores y la contaminación del aire y cumpla con las leyes ambientales de Illinois”.</p><p>La orden judicial le prohíbe a la planta operar hasta al menos el 14 de enero, cuando está programada una audiencia sobre la solicitud de Raoul y la Ciudad para una orden judicial preliminar. Las operaciones permanecerán suspendidas hasta que se emita una orden final.</p><p>“Los miembros de la comunidad alrededor de las instalaciones de Pullman Innovations han soportado una carga demasiado pesada de daño ambiental durante demasiado tiempo, y me complace que por fin tendrán cierto alivio de los malos olores que interrumpían sus vidas y afectaban su capacidad de disfrutar sus hogares y las actividades del vecindario”, dijo Raoul.</p><p>Un abogado de la empresa matriz de Pullman Innovations, A-F Acquisition LLC, no respondió de inmediato a una solicitud de comentarios.</p><p>La planta ha provocado quejas desde antes de que Pullman Innovations tomara el control, incluidas algunas que se remontan a décadas atrás, a una empresa predecesora, Agri-Fine, que anteriormente fue demandada por la exfiscal general Lisa Madigan antes de cerrar sus operaciones.</p><p>El Departamento de Salud Pública de Chicago ha multado anteriormente a Pullman Innovations en varias ocasiones por infracciones al código. Investigadores de la Agencia de Protección Ambiental de Illinois (IEPA) también han confirmado antes el olor tanto dentro de la planta como en los vecindarios cercanos, y en ocasiones se les dificultó respirar.</p><p>Un inspector municipal, cuyo testimonio fue presentado en apoyo de la orden de restricción, dijo que él personalmente había realizado 160 inspecciones en el lugar y describió el olor como un “hedor a huevo podrido, azufrado” que “me ardía en las fosas nasales y me causaba un fuerte dolor de cabeza”.</p><p>Algunos vecinos sugirieron al Chicago Sun-Times en agosto que el olor abrumador podría haber enmascarado el olor de cuerpos en descomposición en la funeraria South Chicago Chapel, que actualmente está bajo investigación.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: An open letter to Pope Leo XIV regarding cancer, and how to survive it
entries.summary: <p>Dear Pope Leo:</p><p>Whenever a friend gets cancer, I usually buy them a copy of "Time on Fire: A Comedy of Terrors," by Evan Handler. The actor's 1996 memoir is an excellent guide to navigating cancer, full of practical tips, such as making sure your nurses wash their hands.</p><p>It's funny, honest, and best of all — spoiler alert! — Handler survives, to this day.</p><p>While I did consider shipping a copy to Rome, I immediately envisioned the package being tossed into one of dozens of huge canvas-sided rolling postal carts jammed with goodwill offerings: prayer cards and inspirational books and charms from the spectrum of faiths. You're a popular guy, as I'm sure you already know.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-620000" name="module-620000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>So I figured, better to drop my advice into this newspaper bottle and toss it into the electronic sea. Perhaps a favorable breeze will nudge it your direction. If not — the sure bet — it might help someone else in a similar position. </p><p>My apologies about giving advice. I have a few rules regarding friends plunged into sickness or misfortune, and Rule No. 1 is: "Don't try to fix things." A rule frequently broken; it's hard to resist trying to help, and hand-washing is so important. People forget, and nice guys such as ourselves, we have a hard time greeting a nurse striding into our room with "Did you wash your hands?"</p><p>I imagine the pope gets first class treatment. Something to be thankful for. Gratitude is key in overcoming travails. My major health troubles have all been mostly mechanical, rather than metastatic — spine, hip and now shoulder — which strikes me as far less severe than the Big C. I try to focus on how lucky I am to have access to advanced medical treatment, as opposed most people in the world, who don't. Attitude is important.</p><p>"A cheerful heart is good medicine," says Proverbs... but look who I'm quoting scripture at. I'm not someone who believes in divine providence. But coincidences happen. Within hours of your lung cancer surgery Tuesday, my older sister, Debbie, arrived from Dallas. I don't write about Debbie much, because she's usually deep in the heart of Texas, arm wrestling the Angel of Death. But she's here now, visiting, and as a true cancer warrior — she's had three kinds over the past 14 years — I asked her for any wisdom she might share with a newbie such as yourself.</p><p>First, she corrected me, not three different cancers, but thyroid cancer that spread to her lungs and led to leukemia — blood cancer — from the high doses of radiation used to fight the first two. Accuracy is important.</p><p>"What specific kind of lung cancer does the pope have?" she asked — a very Debbie question. She's into mastering the research, knowing the latest.</p><p>"I like to be as informed as I can," she explained. "So I can partner with my doctors." </p><p>She said you need to make sure you get the best care. Sure, she could have her treatments nearby, at Parkland hospital in Dallas. And I could have had my spine rebuilt at a CVS MinuteClinic. Instead she flies to MD Anderson, in Houston, a top cancer center. She suggested that, being pope, you might have a shot at getting into Anderson yourself. She'll put in a good word for you, if you like.</p><p>Until then, "stay active" — kind of hard not to, being pope. "Rest when you need to. Sleep is very important."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-630000" name="image-630000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Gregorio Borgia/AP</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Don't be afraid to take decisive action, which is in our family DNA. My sister first got sick at 13 — heart disease — and was a patient at humble Southwest General Hospital in our hometown of Berea, Ohio. Getting sicker and sicker, until our father decided Southwest wasn't working, yanked her out and drove her to Case Western Reserve's Babies and Children's Hospital on the East Side of Cleveland. They received her in one of those high backed wicker wheelchairs with the big wheel in front and the small in back, like in "Heidi," which vaguely terrified me at the time. But they saved her life.</p><p>The hospital might have had help. I don't pray, generally, but now that I recall, I did pray, at the time, for Debbie, down on my knees with my hands clasped in front of me. While I can't imagine the process where that might actually done anything, I suppose it couldn't have hurt.</p><p>I do wish upon stars, which is close to prayer, and the next time I'm out on a clear night and <i>riveder le stelle</i><i>,</i> as Dante, and you, would say, I'll pick a bright one, and ask the indifferent cosmos, "Please heal Pope Leo." Though when you're all better, I assume you'll want to credit your guy, and that's fine with me.</p><p>Your friend,</p><p>Neil Steinberg</p>

entries.title: CPS watchdog closes investigation of school board candidate with ‘no actionable finding of sexual misconduct’
entries.summary: <p>The inspector general’s office at Chicago Public Schools has closed its recently reopened investigation into allegations that school board presidential candidate Hilario Dominguez had inappropriate conduct with a minor in 2017.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://hilarioforcps.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/oig-report_Redacted.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>According to a letter sent to Dominguez Wednesday</u></a> from the CPS Office of Student Protections and Title IX, which Dominguez posted on his campaign website, the inspector general’s office “determined that there is no actionable finding of sexual misconduct.”</p><p>The office made no additional findings regarding possible CPS “policy or guidelines violations relating to this incident.” That letter says the “investigation is concluded and the matter is closed” and that no further action will be taken.</p><p>The letter is not the same as the inspector general’s report, which has yet to be released publicly and will elaborate on why there was no actionable finding.</p><p>The inspector general’s office determined the same allegations were unsubstantiated earlier this year, but <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/10/09/reopened-probe-into-cps-board-president-candidates-alleged-inappropriate-contact-with-teen-could-end-soon" target="_blank" ><u>recently decided to reopen the investigation</u></a>. The young woman who made the allegations said she was not interviewed for the original investigation and came forward because she wanted to tell her story.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://hilarioforcps.com/with-office-of-inspector-general-investigation-announcing-he-is-cleared-in-full-hilario-dominguez-recenters-race-on-competing-visions/" target="_blank" ><u>In a post on Dominguez’s campaign website</u></a>, his lawyer, Rima Kapitan, said the inspector general’s report “fully cleared” Dominguez of any wrongdoing.</p><p>The Dominguez campaign also reiterated that the allegations came from Aida Flores, who was one of Dominguez’s opponents in a race for a City Council seat in 2019. Flores is an assistant principal in CPS and has personal ties to the young woman who made the accusations, according to multiple sources.</p><p>“Voters who weren’t aware of the decade-old smear the Aida Flores campaign spread when I ran for alderman in 2019 deserved an answer to them being brought back this year,” Dominguez <a class="Link" href="https://hilarioforcps.com/with-office-of-inspector-general-investigation-announcing-he-is-cleared-in-full-hilario-dominguez-recenters-race-on-competing-visions/" target="_blank" ><u>wrote in a statement</u></a>. “The OIG [Office of Inspector General] has given it to them.”</p><p>Dominguez said he now wants to “re-center his campaign” on education issues “that voters deeply care about.”</p><p>WBEZ reached out to the young woman, who is now 26, through her lawyer, who did not respond. <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/10/14/chicago-public-schools-watchdog-closes-hilario-dominguez-inquiry/?utm_source=cbnewsletters.chalkbeat.org&utm_medium=newsletter&utm_campaign=no-actionable-finding-in-investigation-of-board-candidate&_bhlid=e2d256ba6a34deab1f53935ee353ae5eb35d69f6" target="_blank" ><u>She told Chalkbeat and Block Club Chicago</u></a> that while she was disappointed in the investigation’s outcome and wanted an outside probe into how the CPS inspector general handled the matter, it had been empowering to share her experience.</p><p>“Young people, your voice still has power, and you may not get justice right away, but always documenting it is important,” she told the news outlets.</p><p>Flores also did not respond to a request for comment.</p><p><i>This story was updated to include comment from the young woman involved in the CPS inspector general’s investigation.</i></p>

entries.title: Barack Obama apoya a Juliana Stratton para el puesto del Senado que dejará Durbin
entries.summary: <p>Declarando que “si puedes triunfar en Springfield, puedes triunfar en Washington, D.C.”, el expresidente Barack Obama respaldó el lunes a Juliana Stratton para el <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/10/01/what-to-know-us-senate-race-juliana-stratton-don-tracy-dick-durbin" target="_blank" >escaño en el Senado de Estados Unidos</a> que quedó vacante tras la jubilación del senador Dick Durbin.</p><p>“Juliana Stratton es una mujer del lado sur, madre, cuidadora y luchadora. Por eso me sentí orgulloso de respaldar su primera campaña para representante estatal y por eso no veo la hora de votar por ella para que sea la próxima senadora por el gran estado de Illinois”, dijo Obama en un video difundido por la campaña de Stratton para el Senado.</p><p>En un inusual respaldo a nivel legislativo estatal, Obama apoyó la candidatura de Stratton a la Cámara de Representantes estatal en 2016 y ayudó a hacer campaña por el gobernador de Illinois, JB Pritzker, y Stratton en 2018 en Urbana y Chicago.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-9e0000" name="module-9e0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Obama ha grabado al menos dos docenas de anuncios para candidatos demócratas a gobernador y al Senado, que se espera sean publicados en los próximos días y semanas. También planea participar en actos de campaña en estados clave.</p><p>La campaña de Stratton dijo que la última vez que ambos se vieron fue en la ceremonia de inauguración del Centro Presidencial Obama el 18 de junio. No se anticipa que Obama aparezca en ningún acto de Stratton antes del Día de las Elecciones.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/AshasSYrQFM?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="President Barack Obama's Message on Juliana Stratton"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Después de ganar su primera campaña política en 2016, Stratton —también originaria del lado sur de Chicago— agradeció a Obama en su discurso de victoria en el vecindario de Bronzeville.</p><p>“Sé que el presidente Barack Obama está aquí en espíritu”, dijo.</p><p>Entre los respaldos que Obama ha dado hasta la fecha están el candidato al Senado por Georgia, Jon Ossoff, el candidato al Senado por Iowa, Josh Turek, el candidato al Senado por Mississippi, Scott Colom y el candidato al Senado por Maine, Troy Jackson. La Associated Press informa que el 24 de octubre aparecerá en Detroit con el candidato al Senado de Estados Unidos por Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed.</p><p>También encabezará un evento del Comité de Campaña Senatorial Demócrata con la senadora de Delaware, Lisa Blunt Rochester, esta semana.</p><p>El respaldo de Obama menciona que Stratton “alzó la voz y contraatacó” durante la campaña de deportaciones del presidente Donald Trump en el área de Chicago, el Operativo Midway Blitz. Stratton estuvo entre un grupo de demócratas de Illinois que <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/01/20/democratas-de-illinois-se-suman-a-los-crecientes-pedidos-de-abolir-ice" target="_blank" >pidió abolir el Servicio de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas</a> (ICE) en enero, y reforzó ese mensaje durante varios mítines y debates.</p><p>Stratton cuenta con el respaldo de Pritzker, Durbin, la senadora Tammy Duckworth y los 14 miembros demócratas de la delegación de la Cámara de Illinois, además de varios otros demócratas.</p><p>En la contienda por el Senado, Stratton se enfrenta al candidato republicano Don Tracy, quien fue expresidente del Partido Republicano de Illinois, y al candidato independiente Whitfield Harrington Jr. La vicegobernadora derrotó a dos miembros demócratas del Congreso —los representantes federales Raja Krishnamoorthi y Robin Kelly— y a otros ocho candidatos en una reñida primaria de marzo.</p><p>Stratton y Tracy tienen previsto participar la próxima semana en un foro de la estación WTTW.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Troy Aikman opens door to leaving Joe Buck, ESPN behind
entries.summary: <p>“Monday Night Football” analyst Troy Aikman left no room for interpretation during a radio appearance Thursday about his status after the season: He’ll be a free agent, and by the sound of it, the NFL’s longest-running pairing is in jeopardy.</p><p>Aikman went on The Ticket (WTCK) in Dallas and was asked about a report by Front Office Sports that said he and “MNF” partner Joe Buck argued before the broadcast Monday after tensions had grown regarding their contracts with ESPN. Buck agreed to a six-year deal last month, according to The Athletic, but Aikman hasn’t received an offer, FOS reported.</p><p>“I don’t know if it’s hard to figure out kind of what has happened,” Aikman said. “I’ll broadcast through this season, and I’ll be a free agent at the end of the year and kind of see what happens. I’m looking forward to whatever the rest of this year does hold and the Super Bowl and all that and where my next landing spot may be.”</p><p>Buck and Aikman have worked together for 25 years, passing Pat Summerall and John Madden as the longest-tenured pair in 2023, their second season at ESPN. At the end of this season, the network will broadcast its first Super Bowl, into which it’s putting seemingly every resource imaginable to promote. A Buck-Aikman rift figures to cast a pall over the run-up.</p><p>In 2 ½ decades together, it’s hard to believe Buck and Aikman never had a spat of some kind. But to hear that this one might play a part in sending Aikman, a Hall of Fame quarterback with the Cowboys, to another network is surprising. He could be angling to bring ESPN to the negotiating table. For whatever reason, the network hasn’t placated him. It might need to do something to address the matter and not let it simmer for four months.</p><p>According to FOS, Buck addressed the tension between him and Aikman in the booth before the Bills-Rams game, leading to an argument. The situation diffused, and viewers were never the wiser.</p><p>If Aikman were to leave ESPN, it could spark changes at other networks. Sports Business Journal reported that Fox hasn’t had contract talks with No. 2 analyst Greg Olsen. At CBS, J.J. Watt’s spot on the No. 1 team with Jim Nantz — which opened when the network dumped Tony Romo after his drunk-driving arrest — is not permanent. Aikman seemingly would have options.</p><p>Aikman also is dabbling in consulting for the Dolphins, opening the possibility that he’d consider joining an NFL front office. However, it’s unlikely that a team would match the $18 million he’s making per year. Buck’s current contract pays him $15 million per year, according to The Athletic, which reported his new deal is worth more than $100 million.</p>

entries.title: Illinois erases $1.4 billion in medical debt for thousands of residents
entries.summary: <p>A statewide effort has so far eliminated more than $1.4 billion in medical debt for thousands of Illinois residents, Gov. JB Pritzker announced Thursday at a news conference.</p><p>Pritzker touted the results of the state’s Medical Debt Relief Program, which started about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2024/04/15/jb-pritzker-medical-debt-relief-erase-1-billion-toni-preckwinkle" target="_blank" ><u>two years ago</u></a>. The state had allocated $10 million toward the program, and Pritzker said in the Cook County Health building that he’s committed to continuing funding for the program.</p><p>“One of the great things about this program is that the return on investment is so high,” Pritzker said. “Every penny that we put in relieves a dollar of debt. I don’t know any other program that has that kind of return for people.”</p><p>Pritzker said the program aims to address the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/06/19/hospital-billing-transparency-federal-law-failed-consumer-health7" target="_blank" ><u>unaffordable financial burden</u></a> residents are saddled with because of an unexpected injury or illness. The state program has reached 694,000 residents, according to Pritzker's office. On average, residents had about $1,200 in debt eliminated though one person had as much as $900,000 in medical debt erased, according to the state.</p><p>Pritzker was joined by Cook County Board President Toni Preckwinkle who first implemented a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2025/06/05/cook-county-erases-nearly-665-million-in-medical-debt-for-more-than-a-half-million-residents" target="_blank" ><u>medical debt relief program in the county</u></a>. The state and county programs combined have eliminated $2.4 billion in debt for about 1.5 million residents, according to the state and county officials.</p><p>Cook County used federal funds from the American Rescue Plan Act to start the local program, but Preckwinkle also said she’s committed to continue funding the initiative once those federal funds end.</p><p>“The next phase of this work will put data from this initiative to use to understand who is being pushed into medical debt and why, and to design policies that address its root causes,” Preckwinkle said.</p><p>The state and county have worked with <a class="Link" href="https://unduemedicaldebt.org/government-partnerships/" target="_blank" ><u>Undue Medical Debt</u></a>, a nonprofit that negotiates the sale or donation of portfolios of medical debt with hospitals and health systems. Eligible households typically have to have an income at or below 400% of the federal poverty level.</p><p>The program stands out from others in that residents do not apply for it. Instead, a person who’s had their medical debt eliminated by the state or county programs receives a letter in the mail notifying them of how much debt was erased, Pritzker said.</p><p>“I’ve talked to some folks who’ve received a letter like that; people have broken out crying,” Pritzker said. “People want to pay their debts. They do and they get bills in the mail that they know they are obligated, that they’re supposed to pay, and with medical debt, they often just can’t — it’s too much.”</p><p>In suburban DuPage County, about 7% of residents had debt erased by the state’s program. Nearly 13% of Kane County residents had medical debt eliminated along with nearly 9% of residents in Lake County. About 22% of residents in Kankakee County, about 60 miles south of Chicago, had their medical debt eliminated as well.</p>

entries.title: Is Bears QB Caleb Williams playing vs. Falcons on Sunday? He talks for first time since hamstring injury
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/11/as-engineer-and-artist-blend-styles-bears-ben-johnson-gets-goosebumps-about-future-with-caleb-williams" >Caleb Williams</a> practiced in full Thursday, which further points toward him returning from his hamstring injury Sunday against the Falcons.</p><p>He went through individual drills wearing a black sleeve on his right leg during the part of practice open to the media and looked agile as he worked on pocket footwork and threw on the run. There was no discernible difference in his gait.</p><p>Here’s what Williams said Thursday in his first public comments since getting hurt Sept. 20 against the Vikings:</p><p>- He doesn't know if he'll get the green light to play against the Falcons. Williams added that the injury has not fully healed, but there are "certain parameters that allow you to go out there and play" and "lower the risk of re-injuring."</p><p>- He said he has been able to cut, plant and run without any issues and expects to play to his usual form.</p><p>"I can move," he said. "I can run. I hit a top speed the other day, one of my highest speeds I've ever hit... I've got strength."</p><p>- Williams objected strongly to the reporting on his injury over the past month, saying none of it has been accurate. He said he suffered “a tear” in his hamstring, but refused to reveal the grade of the injury. That’s very relevant, because hamstring strains range are categorized as Grade 1, 2 or 3, with a Grade 3 being the most severe.</p><p>He has been reported to have a Grade 2 hamstring strain, and missing roughly a month lines up with the typical recovery time for that. A Grade 1 includes some minor tearing, while a Grade 3 is a complete tear of the muscle.</p><p>“It’s been fun to deal with because... there’s nothing that has come out that has been right about what it is," he said. "If you haven’t heard it from [Ben Johnson] or me, it would probably be wrong, which every single one has been.</p><p>“It was a situation where, I wouldn’t say that I wanted it, but it was nice for me to be able to learn from Case and Tyson and see how they go about their week. I haven’t been in his position, so it’s been interesting.”</p><p>The only specifics he gave Thursday were that, "It was a hamstring tear, and a pretty serious one." When asked why he wouldn't clarify the injury Thursday, he said, "I wouldn't say it's deserved to be out there."</p><p>- Regarding the criticism that he was overdramatic about the injury when he left Soldier Field in tears, Williams made no apology for being emotional. He did not know in the moment whether the injury was season-ending.</p><p>"My character's been attacked for a while," he said. "It's just another motivating factor."</p>

entries.title: Chance the Rapper prevails again in ongoing legal battle with former manager
entries.summary: <p>Chance the Rapper claimed another legal victory against his former manager, Pat Corcoran, in Cook County Circuit Court this week after a judge ruled the rapper’s former friend and business partner breached his fiduciary duty.</p><p>Corcoran, aka Pat the Manager, had worked for the rapper from the beginnings of his career in 2012 through his termination in 2020 and has been ordered to forfeit merchandise commissions and management fees as well as return the ChanceRaps.com website domain to the artist by Oct. 28. A final hearing is set for Nov. 30, when the specific dollar amount owed to Chance the Rapper will be determined, which could total up to $1.5 million. According to the ruling, over the years he paid Corcoran a share of his net profits, totaling more than $10 million.</p><p>“Merchandise was at the center of what Bennett paid Corcoran to do, which makes this conduct a breach of the core duty,” Judge James Hanlon said in the ruling.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>A judge ruled this week that Pat Corcoran, former manager for Chance the Rapper, “owed” the rapper loyalty on merchandise but “that outside ventures like the Ramova Theatre, We Are the Times, and the Hope film were not part of the bargain,” Hanlon said in the ruling.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“I’m grateful to finally close this chapter of my life and can’t wait to eventually tell my side of the story,” Chance the Rapper, born Chancellor Bennett, said in a statement. “I’m thankful to the courts and, more importantly, to God for remaining faithful.”</p><p>Hanlon wrote that “Each side asks for too much.” While Hanlon sided with Bennett, he denied the rapper’s requests for relief on outside ventures, including music distributor UnitedMasters, media venture We Are the Times, a film project called “Hope” and the Ramova Theatre in Bridgeport, in which Bennett has an ownership stake.</p><p>“Corcoran owed Bennett loyalty [on the merchandise]; he did not owe Bennett the right of first refusal on every investment that came across his desk,” Hanlon said in the ruling.</p><p>A spokesperson for Corcoran’s legal team at Sweeney Scharkey LLC said in a statement to the Sun-Times, “The court ruled there is no basis for Chance’s claim of more than $10 million in damages. We are pleased that the court agreed with Pat that he ‘performed years of valuable work that Bennett accepted and profited from, work that was not self-dealing.’ It is now up to Chance to prove he incurred any harm at all in the very limited areas of merchandising outlined in the order."</p><p>This week’s ruling marks the latest in the ongoing legal drama between the two parties, which originally stemmed from a 2020 lawsuit filed by Corcoran seeking $3.8 million in unpaid commissions after he was fired following a falling out over the lukewarm response to Bennett’s “Big Day Out” album, released in 2019.</p><p>Corcoran stipulated the two had a “sunset clause” that entitled him to royalties for three years post-termination. Bennett countered that they had no such arrangement. The two former friends, once the model for a successful independent artist and manager relationship, operated on a handshake deal and had nothing in writing. Bennett countersued for breach of contract, tortious interference and breach of fiduciary duty, seeking $1 million. In his claim, the music artist alleged Corcoran accepted kickbacks from vendors and partners.</p><p>The<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/03/10/chance-the-rapper-pat-corcoran-trial-lawsuit" target="_blank" ><u> jury trial,</u></a> to determine the basis of the legal claims, took place in March. The jury ruled <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/03/20/chance-rapper-former-manager-lawsuit-pat-corcoran-verdict" target="_blank" ><u>in favor of Bennett,</u></a> throwing out Corcoran’s case and awarding the rapper a nominal $35 in his countersuit as well as the return of the ChanceRaps.com website owned by Corcoran. The bench trial was to determine the fiduciary duty claim.</p><p>The court has given the two parties the chance to settle on a dollar amount by Nov. 30; if one can’t be reached, the court will decide.</p>

entries.title: Private event venue planned for 96th floor of former Hancock building
entries.summary: <p>A new private event venue atop the former John Hancock Center will begin accepting bookings in early 2027, ahead of its planned opening in 2028, 360 Chicago announced on Thursday.</p><p>The nearly 14,000-square-foot space, called Elevaire Chicago, will occupy the 96th floor of 875 N. Michigan Ave., offering views of Lake Michigan and the city's skyline. It will be available for weddings, corporate meetings, networking receptions, galas and other events.</p><p>“Our goal is to create an experience that is deeply personal and unlike any other venue in Chicago,” Nichole Benolken, managing director at 360 Chicago, said in a news release.</p><p>Details about the venue’s capacity, food and beverage offerings, room configurations and event packages will be announced before the venue begins accepting bookings, according to the company.</p><p>The venue is part of a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/entertainment-culture/2025/06/12/former-signature-room-space-hancock-building-transformation-expansion" >broader expansion by 360 Chicago</a>, which operates the building’s 94th-floor observation deck. The company plans to extend its popular attraction into the 95th and 96th floors, eventually creating more than 50,000 square feet of space that the company calls Chicago’s "first multistory observation deck."</p><p>The 95th floor will have additional visitor space and programming. A three-story staircase overlooking Lake Michigan will connect the floors.</p><p>The expansion will transform the two-level space formerly occupied by the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/business/2023/9/28/23894588/signature-room-closes-magnificent-mile-john-hancock-center" >Signature Room</a>, a restaurant and lounge that closed in September 2023 after more than 30 years. </p><p>While the full-service restaurant is gone, visitors can still enjoy drinks, cocktails and snacks at CloudBar, a ticket-required bar on the 94th floor.</p><p>Magnicity, the Paris-based parent company of 360 Chicago, acquired the space in 2024 and announced its expansion plans the following year. The company has hired Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, the architecture firm that designed the building, to lead the renovation.</p>

entries.title: Bulls guard Tre Jones sees a second unit loaded with weapons and talent
entries.summary: <p>There are times where Tre Jones actually feels like it’s “choose your weapon.”</p><p>If the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls" >Bulls</a> reserve guard wants an athletic wing to feed the ball to on the break, look no further than Leonard Miller and his continued rise this preseason.</p><p>If he needs a three to keep the defense spaced, enter Buddy Hield.</p><p>If he wants to play pick-and-roll with a big body, well, he’s seen enough of Zach Collins through the years to know that option is alive and well.</p><p>And when it’s time to keep the ball in his own hands there are few on the roster that are better at attacking the rim with a ridiculous angle game than Jones.</p><p>Yes, Jones is the conductor of Tiago Splitter’s second unit and it’s starting to feel like a group that could be the difference between being a basement dweller this season or actually surprising the league.</p><p>Case in point? Just the last two preseason games alone, as Jones and company kicked the tempo into high gear to help pull away from Milwaukee on Wednesday, just a few nights removed from outscoring Denver’s bench 75-56 on Sunday.</p><p>“Hundred percent, 100%,” Splitter said when asked about if the bench could be a game changer for the Bulls this season. “We change the pace. They play so fast it just changes the whole thing. You got a lot of guys that can push the pace and be aggressive.”</p><p>But it all starts with the high-IQ of Jones.</p><p>There’s a reason why Jones was Billy Donovan’s favorite player, evident by last season alone when he led the Bulls in total win share (5.7). He can play fast, he can play slow, he can help rookies mature and he knows how to keep fellow veterans happy.</p><p>Jones has also been around the Association since 2020, raised out of college by Spurs culture, much like his coach was.</p><p>He knows a solid bench when he sees it.</p><p>“I think our second unit can be really good,” Jones said. “If we want to be really good as a team our second unit needs to be that good and hold ourselves to that standard. The energy that the second unit brings will be key for us. We’re really unselfish in that group, we share the ball. We really don’t care who scores as long as we score as a unit, that’s all that matters. We try to build off our defense. We’ve got the length and athleticism so try to use that to our advantage and get stops, feed off of that.”</p><p>No wonder intrasquad scrimmages have been so cutthroat throughout training camp.</p><p>Not only is that second unit competitive but it almost mirrors the makeup of that first unit. Jones doesn’t have Josh Giddey’s size, but he has his pass-first mentality and ability to push the group with pace. Leonard, Isaac Okoro and Noa Essengue might not have the bounce of starters Matas Buzelis and Caleb Wilson, but they are athletic wings that love to run.</p><p>Hield is no Norman Powell, but they are both a bucket that can stretch the floor.</p><p>“I Feel like we do mirror each other – the first and second units – a little bit,” Jones said. “You got a little bit of similar everywhere, and yeah, scrimmages, practices, we’ve been going at it. That only makes you better. We’ve got another week or so to hone in on the things we want to do better before this thing really starts.”</p><p>What Jones wants to make sure this group does better is continue holding it to a standard, starting with himself.</p><p>“I take pride in that, for sure, trying to run that group,” he added. “We’ve shown the last couple of games we could be really good, and we just have to build off of that. Just a lot weapons.”</p>

entries.title: CATCH-22: Bears facing starting lefty QB for second time in 15 years
entries.summary: <p>Analyzing the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" >Bears</a> with the help of 22 names, starting with …</p><p><b>Michael Penix (1)</b>, who will be the rarest of Bears opponents on Sunday — a left-handed quarterback. The Bears have faced one lefty starter in the last 15 years — <b>Tua Tagovailoa</b> (2) in Week 9 of 2022. Even if Penix somehow doesn’t start — the Falcons say his ribs are fine — his backup is, you guessed it, Tagovailoa.</p><p>About one-in-10 people are left-handed. Yet just 11 of the 426 regular-season games the Bears have played since 2000 have had an opposing lefty under center. That’s 2.6% of their games.</p><p>League-wide, only three lefties have started at quarterback since 2020: Penix, Tagovailoa and the Browns’ <b>Dillon Gabriel (3)</b>. Falcons coach <b>Kevin Stefanski (4)</b> has coached all three. Five other lefty quarterbacks started a game in the 2010s.</p><p>Bears defensive backs coach <b>Al Harris (5)</b> and nickelbacks coach <b>Cannon Matthews</b> <b>(6)</b> were watching film this week and commented on how strange it was to see a lefty passer.</p><p>“The ball just comes out different. …” Harris said. “Just the way the ball spins.”</p><p>A football spins about 600 times per minute. The gyroscopic torque of the ball pushes the ball right when it is thrown by a right-hander and left when thrown by a left-hander.</p><p>“Everything just looks foreign — it looks weird,” Matthews said.</p><p>Falcons offensive coordinator <b>Tommy Rees (7)</b>, the former Lake Forest High School and Notre Dame star, flipped his standard plays this offseason to make them more lefty-friendly.</p><p>The Bears’ reeling defense won’t do the same.</p><p>“We’re not spending a ton of time talking about, scheming up, for a left-handed quarterback,” defensive coordinator <b>Dennis Allen</b> <b>(8)</b> said.</p><p>The team has focused on adjusting to angles of the lefty passes this week, though. They have a secret weapon. Assistant linebackers coach <b>Kevin Koch</b> <b>(9)</b> was a left-handed quarterback at Immaculate Conception High School in Elmhurst, the College of DuPage and Minnesota-State Moorhead. He’s thrown passes during practices all year — and particularly this week.</p><p>“We get those simulations in walk-through,” Matthews said.</p><h3><b>Someone familiar with the left-hander’s spin is …</b></h3><h3></h3><p><b>Rome Odunze (10)</b>, who spent the last two years of his college career catching passes from the same man the Bears face Sunday. Odunze and Penix formed one of the best pass-catching duos in recent college football history in 2023, when the latter led all FBS receivers with a University of Washington-record 1,640 receiving yards. Odunze was Penix’s leading receiver in the Huskies’ national championship game loss to Michigan in January 2024.</p><p>Odunze learned to adjust for Penix’s spin on the fly. A lefty passer was rare, even in college — in 2024, the year after Odunze went pro, only five of the 131 qualifying quarterbacks in FBS threw from the left-handed side.</p><p>“It’s a little different,” the Bears receiver said. “There’s a little bit different torque on the ball. … There were times in windy games at [Washington] it did tail differently.”</p><p>Odunze said he was proud to see Penix return from his third torn ACL to boost the Falcons, starting in Week 3. The Falcons were 0-2 before his return but are 2-1 since, with their lone loss coming after Tagovailoa threw an overtime interception in relief of Penix on Sunday night.</p><p>“That’s been the story at different levels of his career …” Odunze said. “People were writing him off after this last injury as well, but I’m like, ‘Man, that’s when Penix shines — when people are doubting him and he’s coming off that injury.’ Because people have doubted him before.”</p><h3><b>Friday is the 20th anniversary of …</b></h3><h3></h3><p><b>Dennis Green’s</b> <b>(11) </b>“crown their ass” speech, minutes after the Bears rallied from a 23-3 deficit with the help of two defensive scores and one special teams touchdown to beat the Cardinals 24-23. <b>Devin Hester</b> <b>(12),</b> then a rookie, returned a punt for an 83-yard touchdown with about three minutes to play to seal the win. The Cardinals’ starting quarterback: southpaw <b>Matt Leinart (13)</b>. In the 20 years since, the Bears have faced four other lefty starters: the Eagles’ <b>Michael Vick (14)</b> twice plus the Chiefs’ <b>Tyler Palko</b> <b>(15)</b>, the Broncos’ <b>Tim Tebow (16)</b> and Tagovailoa.</p><h3><b>The last Bears lefty to start at quarterback was. …</b></h3><h3></h3><p><b>Cade McNown</b> <b>(17)</b>, who went 3-12 in two dreadful seasons here. Their most established was <b>Bobby Douglass (18)</b>, the run-first quarterback who played for the Bears from 1969-75.</p><h3><b>But were any of them left-handed?</b></h3><p>Sunday will be the third time the Bears have ever played at Mercedes-Benz Stadium. The other two, fittingly, have marked changes in the Bears’ quarterback saga. I was the only Chicago media member in attendance in 2020, when <b>Mitch Trubisky (19)</b> was benched in the third quarter in favor of <b>Nick Foles (20)</b>, who famously told receiver <b>Anthony Miller</b> <b>(21)</b> to “run to the L” in the end zone for the game-winning touchdown pass. Quarterback <b>Justin Fields (22)</b> hurt his shoulder late in his 2023 homecoming and was forced to miss the next game.</p>
